docs.title: Complex Routing (Kafka)
docs.text:
Records often belong in different Kafka topics: task events in one, telemetry in another, and alarms in a topic that someone watches. KafkaEgress takes a topic_router function that picks the topic for each record, instead of one event topic and one telemetry topic.

With a router, KafkaEgress does not create topics at start, because only the router knows which ones it uses, so create them first. The snippets below publish to Kafka, so start a broker first with odctl up kafka-lite. See Installation for the one-time odctl install. Tear it down with odctl down kafka-lite --volumes.

docs.title: Writing a Custom Router
docs.text:
A topic router is a Python function that receives one record, as a dictionary with its stream_type, key or path_id, task, instance and value, and returns the topic name as a string. KafkaEgress sends every record it receives, so the router must always return a topic. To drop records, give the provider a when predicate on add_egress, which filters them before they reach the router.

This router sends telemetry, alarms and other events to three topics:

docs/snippets/guides/complex_routing.py:router
def custom_kafka_router(data: Dict[str, Any]) -> str:
    """Picks a topic for each record by its kind and its value."""
    if data.get("stream_type") == "telemetry":
        return "shop-telemetry"

    value = data.get("value")
    if isinstance(value, dict) and (
        value.get("status") == "packing_failed" or value.get("level") == "ERROR"
    ):
        return "system-alarms"

    # Every other event, including a payload that is not a dict.
    return "shop-events"

docs.title: Attaching the Router
docs.text:
Pass the router as topic_router to KafkaEgress:

docs/snippets/guides/complex_routing.py:egress
app = (
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
    .add_egress(
        KafkaEgress(
            bootstrap_servers="localhost:9092",
            topic_router=custom_kafka_router,
        )
    )
)

docs.title: Run the Shop
docs.text:
The shop packs an order about every 2 seconds, and every tenth order fails, so all three topics receive records. The minimal statistics give shop-telemetry a reading every 10 seconds:

docs/snippets/guides/complex_routing.py:shop
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
app.add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
app.with_stats("minimal", interval=10)  # readings for shop-telemetry


@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    if task_id % 10 == 9:  # every tenth order fails, for system-alarms
        return {"status": "packing_failed"}
    return {"status": "packed"}


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def orders(context: SimulationContext):
    while True:
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(context.next_instance("pack_order"), entity=order))

Before the run, the script creates the three topics with KafkaAdminConnector:

docs/snippets/guides/complex_routing.py:run
if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
    )
    # With a router, KafkaEgress creates no topics, so create them first
    admin = KafkaAdminConnector(bootstrap_servers="localhost:9092")
    admin.create_topics([{"name": topic} for topic in TOPICS])
    app.run(until="1 min")

Run it with python complex_routing.py while kafka-lite is up. The Kafka UI of kafka-lite, at http://127.0.0.1:8086, shows the records arriving in shop-events, shop-telemetry and system-alarms.

docs.title: Full Script
Dynamic Topology: Resources Changed Mid-run
docs.text:
Sometimes the layout itself changes during a run: a dock opens a new bay, or a shop adds a gift wrapping station. Here a supervisor process adds gift wrappers at 12 seconds, and from then on new jobs go to the wrappers as well as the packers.

The builder (SimulationContext) creates every resource before the clock starts and has no call to add one later. A resource added during the run is written with the low-level API: register its parameters, then create the DynamicResource that reads them.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
docs/snippets/guides/dynamic_topology.py
import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)

WORK = 3.0  # seconds each job takes
NEW_JOBS_EVERY = 4.0  # seconds between rounds of new jobs
ADD_WRAPPERS_AT = 12.0  # simulation time at which the gift wrappers are added

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=5)},
)


def worker(env, resources, name, job_id):
    resource = resources[name]
    key = f"{name}-{job_id}"
    env.publish_event(key, {"resource": name, "status": "queued"})
    with resource.request() as req:
        yield req
        env.publish_event(key, {"resource": name, "status": "started"})
        yield env.timeout(WORK)
        env.publish_event(key, {"resource": name, "status": "finished"})


def supervisor(env, resources):
    job_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(NEW_JOBS_EVERY)

        if env.now >= ADD_WRAPPERS_AT and "wrappers" not in resources:
            # Give the gift wrappers their registry paths, then create the resource
            # that reads its capacity from them.
            env.registry.register_sim_parameter(
                SimParameter(
                    sim_id="Shop",
                    resources={"wrappers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=2, max_cap=5)},
                )
            )
            resources["wrappers"] = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "wrappers")
            env.publish_event(
                "supervisor",
                {
                    "status": "wrappers_added",
                    "capacity": resources["wrappers"].capacity,
                },
            )

        # One new job for every resource that exists now.
        for name in list(resources):
            env.process(worker(env, resources, name, job_id))
        job_id += 1


def run(until=20.0, factor=1.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])

    resources = {"packers": DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")}
    env.process(supervisor(env, resources))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()  # flushes the buffers and stops the threads
    return resources


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

Save it as dynamic_topology.py and run python dynamic_topology.py. It runs for 20 seconds in real time (factor=1.0) and prints each event.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
• PARAMS registers only the packers when the run starts.
  • supervisor wakes every NEW_JOBS_EVERY seconds. At ADD_WRAPPERS_AT it calls env.registry.register_sim_parameter with a SimParameter that holds only the wrappers, which adds the paths Shop.resources.wrappers.current_cap and Shop.resources.wrappers.max_cap. It then creates DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "wrappers"), which reads its capacity from those paths, and publishes wrappers_added.
  • New jobs are started for every resource in resources, so the wrappers get jobs from the round in which they are added.
  • worker is one job: it publishes queued, started and finished with the resource it used.
  • run creates the environment, starts the supervisor and calls env.teardown() at the end, which writes the records still in the buffers.

The wrappers' capacity is live like any other. A scenario, a connector or a process can change Shop.resources.wrappers.current_cap once the path exists, as Live Parameters describes.

docs.title: Connecting to Secure Kafka Clusters
docs.text:
The Kafka connectors pass any keyword argument they do not use themselves to the Kafka client underneath, so SASL, mTLS, OAuth and AWS IAM work without code of your own. KafkaIngress and KafkaEgress use aiokafka. KafkaAdminConnector uses kafka-python for create_topics and aiokafka for send_config and collect_data, so its arguments must suit the library each method uses.

Every example here connects to a managed or secured cluster. No odctl profile runs a secured broker, so the full script at the end needs a cluster of your own that uses SASL PLAIN, such as Confluent Cloud. To try the connectors locally without security, start a broker with odctl up kafka-lite and see Installation.

docs.title: Confluent Cloud (SASL PLAIN)
docs.text:
For Confluent Cloud, or any cluster that uses SASL PLAIN or SCRAM, pass security_protocol, sasl_mechanism and the credentials:

docs/snippets/guides/kafka_security.py:sasl
egress = KafkaEgress(
    bootstrap_servers="pkc-xxxx.us-east-1.aws.confluent.cloud:9092",
    # Passed as they are to the Kafka client
    security_protocol="SASL_SSL",
    sasl_mechanism="PLAIN",  # or SCRAM-SHA-512
    sasl_plain_username="<YOUR_API_KEY>",
    sasl_plain_password="<YOUR_API_SECRET>",
)

With no topic_router, KafkaEgress creates sim-events and sim-telemetry when it starts, and passes the security settings to the admin client that creates them.

docs.title: On-Premise Cluster (mTLS)
docs.text:
For a cluster that requires mutual TLS, build an SSL context from your certificate files. aiokafka takes only ssl_context, not the certificate paths, and kafka-python accepts the same context, so one context serves every connector.

docs/snippets/guides/kafka_security.py:mtls
from aiokafka.helpers import create_ssl_context

from desflow import KafkaIngress

ssl_context = create_ssl_context(
    cafile="/path/to/ca.pem",
    certfile="/path/to/service.cert",
    keyfile="/path/to/service.key",
)

ingress = KafkaIngress(
    topic="sim-commands",
    bootstrap_servers="secure-broker.internal.company.com:9093",
    security_protocol="SSL",
    ssl_context=ssl_context,
)

docs.title: AWS MSK (IAM)
docs.text:
Amazon MSK with IAM access control uses sasl_mechanism="OAUTHBEARER" with a token provider. The token comes from the aws-msk-iam-sasl-signer-python package, which you install yourself.

Each library checks the provider's type. aiokafka requires a subclass of aiokafka.abc.AbstractTokenProvider with an async token(). kafka-python requires a subclass of kafka.sasl.oauth.AbstractTokenProvider with a plain token(). One object cannot be both, so the connectors that use aiokafka get one provider, and create_topics gets the other.

docs/snippets/guides/kafka_security.py:msk
from aiokafka.abc import AbstractTokenProvider as AsyncTokenProvider
from aws_msk_iam_sasl_signer import MSKAuthTokenProvider
from kafka.sasl.oauth import AbstractTokenProvider as SyncTokenProvider

from desflow import KafkaAdminConnector, KafkaEgress

def msk_token() -> str:
    # Uses the AWS credentials of your environment, or the EC2 or EKS role
    token, _ = MSKAuthTokenProvider.generate_auth_token("us-east-1")
    return token

class AsyncMSKTokenProvider(AsyncTokenProvider):
    async def token(self):
        return msk_token()

class SyncMSKTokenProvider(SyncTokenProvider):
    def token(self):
        return msk_token()

msk = dict(
    bootstrap_servers="b-1.my-msk.amazonaws.com:9098",
    security_protocol="SASL_SSL",
    sasl_mechanism="OAUTHBEARER",
)

# KafkaIngress and KafkaEgress use aiokafka
egress = KafkaEgress(
    **msk, topic_router=my_router, sasl_oauth_token_provider=AsyncMSKTokenProvider()
)

# create_topics uses kafka-python
admin = KafkaAdminConnector(**msk, sasl_oauth_token_provider=SyncMSKTokenProvider())
admin.create_topics([{"name": "sim-events", "partitions": 3}])

The same OAUTHBEARER setting works with a token provider of your own for Okta, Auth0 or another single sign-on provider.

docs.title: Use It in a Simulation
docs.text:
A connector with security settings is added like any other. This simulation publishes its events through the SASL egress above:

docs/snippets/guides/kafka_security.py:shop
app = (
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0, random_seed=42)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
    .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
    .add_egress(egress)  # the SASL egress above
)


@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def orders(context: SimulationContext):
    while True:
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(context.next_instance("pack_order"), entity=order))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
    )
    app.run(until="1 min")

Put your broker address and credentials in egress, then run python kafka_security.py. It runs for one minute.

docs.title: Full Script
docs.text:
Full script

The complete file. It needs a Kafka cluster that uses SASL PLAIN:

docs/snippets/guides/kafka_security.py
"""The secured Kafka connections of the Secure Kafka page, and a shop that uses one.

The simulation publishes to a cluster that uses SASL PLAIN, such as Confluent Cloud: put your
broker address and credentials in the `sasl` section, then run `python
kafka_security.py`. The mTLS and MSK examples read certificate files or call AWS, so
they sit in functions this file defines and does not call.
"""

import logging

from desflow import KafkaEgress, SimulationContext


def my_router(data: dict) -> str:
    return "sim-telemetry" if data.get("stream_type") == "telemetry" else "sim-events"


egress = KafkaEgress(
    bootstrap_servers="pkc-xxxx.us-east-1.aws.confluent.cloud:9092",
    # Passed as they are to the Kafka client
    security_protocol="SASL_SSL",
    sasl_mechanism="PLAIN",  # or SCRAM-SHA-512
    sasl_plain_username="<YOUR_API_KEY>",
    sasl_plain_password="<YOUR_API_SECRET>",
)


def mtls_ingress():
    from aiokafka.helpers import create_ssl_context

    from desflow import KafkaIngress

    ssl_context = create_ssl_context(
        cafile="/path/to/ca.pem",
        certfile="/path/to/service.cert",
        keyfile="/path/to/service.key",
    )

    ingress = KafkaIngress(
        topic="sim-commands",
        bootstrap_servers="secure-broker.internal.company.com:9093",
        security_protocol="SSL",
        ssl_context=ssl_context,
    )
    return ingress


def msk_connectors():
    from aiokafka.abc import AbstractTokenProvider as AsyncTokenProvider
    from aws_msk_iam_sasl_signer import MSKAuthTokenProvider
    from kafka.sasl.oauth import AbstractTokenProvider as SyncTokenProvider

    from desflow import KafkaAdminConnector, KafkaEgress

    def msk_token() -> str:
        # Uses the AWS credentials of your environment, or the EC2 or EKS role
        token, _ = MSKAuthTokenProvider.generate_auth_token("us-east-1")
        return token

    class AsyncMSKTokenProvider(AsyncTokenProvider):
        async def token(self):
            return msk_token()

    class SyncMSKTokenProvider(SyncTokenProvider):
        def token(self):
            return msk_token()

    msk = dict(
        bootstrap_servers="b-1.my-msk.amazonaws.com:9098",
        security_protocol="SASL_SSL",
        sasl_mechanism="OAUTHBEARER",
    )

    # KafkaIngress and KafkaEgress use aiokafka
    egress = KafkaEgress(
        **msk, topic_router=my_router, sasl_oauth_token_provider=AsyncMSKTokenProvider()
    )

    # create_topics uses kafka-python
    admin = KafkaAdminConnector(**msk, sasl_oauth_token_provider=SyncMSKTokenProvider())
    admin.create_topics([{"name": "sim-events", "partitions": 3}])
    return egress, admin


app = (
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0, random_seed=42)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
    .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
    .add_egress(egress)  # the SASL egress above
)


@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def orders(context: SimulationContext):
    while True:
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(context.next_instance("pack_order"), entity=order))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
    )
    app.run(until="1 min")

docs.title: Multi-Resource Handoffs
docs.text:
A handoff passes an order from one resource to the next without letting go of the first too early. Here a picker carries each order to a packing bench. The order keeps the picker until the bench is free, so for a moment it holds both, and then it releases the picker.

@app.task requests one resource, holds it for the service time and releases it. An order that holds two resources at once, and releases them at different times, needs a task written as a generator that you start with context.spawn.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
docs/snippets/guides/multi_resource_handoffs.py
import logging

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)

WALK = 1.0  # seconds the picker takes to carry an order to the packing bench
PACKING = 4.0  # seconds of packing per order

app = (
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0)
    .add_resource("picker", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
    .add_resource("bench", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=1.0)
    .add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
)


def handoff_worker(context: SimulationContext, order, task_id: int):
    picker = context.get_resource("picker")
    bench = context.get_resource("bench")

    def publish(value):
        # Keyed by the order, orders-1 and so on, with the task and its instance id
        context.env.publish_event(order.key, value, task="handoff", instance=task_id)

    publish({"status": "queued"})

    # The picker is released by hand below, not by a `with` block, because the
    # handoff happens in the middle of the bench's block.
    yield picker.request()
    publish({"status": "picked"})
    yield context.env.timeout(WALK)

    # Ask for the bench while still holding the picker.
    with bench.request() as bench_req:
        yield bench_req
        publish({"status": "at_bench"})
        picker.release()  # the order is on the bench, so the picker is free
        yield context.env.timeout(PACKING)
        publish({"status": "finished"})


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def arrival_loop(context: SimulationContext):
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(handoff_worker(context, order, task_id))
        task_id += 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(until=30.0)

Save it as multi_resource_handoffs.py and run python multi_resource_handoffs.py. It runs for 30 seconds in real time (factor=1.0) and prints each event.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
• handoff_worker is one order. It publishes each event with the order's key, orders-1 and so on, and with the task name handoff and its instance id. It publishes queued, waits for the picker, publishes picked and spends WALK seconds on the way to the bench.
  • Asking for the bench happens inside the picker's hold: the order waits for the bench while it still has the picker. When it gets the bench it publishes at_bench and calls picker.release(), so the next order can use the picker. It is packed for PACKING seconds, publishes finished and releases the bench when its with block ends.
  • picker.request() is not in a with block, because a with block would release the picker at its end, after the packing. The picker is released by hand instead.
  • arrival_loop starts a handoff_worker for each arriving order. Orders arrive about once a second and packing takes 4 seconds, so the bench is the bottleneck. An order that waits for the bench keeps the picker, and the orders behind it wait for the picker.

docs.title: Preemptive Breakdowns
docs.text:
A preemptive breakdown stops a machine in the middle of a job. Here a label printer jams while it prints an order's shipping label. The order remains assigned to the printer during repairs, then labelling resumes. No other order can start while the printer is down.

@app.task waits out the service time inside its own generator, so your code cannot catch a simpy.Interrupt there. A breakdown needs a task written as a generator that you start with context.spawn, and a process that interrupts it.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
docs/snippets/guides/preemptive_breakdowns.py
import logging

import simpy

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)

LABELLING = 5.0  # seconds to print and attach the shipping label of one order
REPAIR = 10.0  # seconds the printer is down after a jam
JAM_EVERY = 12.0  # seconds between jams

app = (
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0)
    .add_resource("printer", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.2)
    .add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
)

# The process of the order being labelled, if any, so a jam can interrupt it.
on_printer = []


def worker_task(context: SimulationContext, order, task_id: int):
    printer = context.get_resource("printer")

    def publish(value):
        # Keyed by the order, orders-1 and so on, with the task and its instance id
        context.env.publish_event(order.key, value, task="label", instance=task_id)

    publish({"status": "queued"})

    with printer.request() as req:
        yield req
        publish({"status": "started"})
        remaining = LABELLING
        while remaining > 0:
            on_printer.append(context.env.active_process)
            began = context.env.now
            try:
                yield context.env.timeout(remaining)
                remaining = 0
            except simpy.Interrupt as interrupt:
                remaining -= context.env.now - began
                publish({"status": "interrupted", "cause": interrupt.cause})
            on_printer.remove(context.env.active_process)
            if remaining > 0:
                # The order stays on the printer, so no other order can start, and a
                # printer under repair cannot jam again.
                yield context.env.timeout(REPAIR)
                publish({"status": "printer_repaired"})
        publish({"status": "finished"})


def chaos_monkey(context: SimulationContext):
    while True:
        yield context.env.timeout(JAM_EVERY)
        if on_printer:  # an idle printer has nothing to interrupt
            on_printer[0].interrupt("paper_jam")


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def arrival_loop(context: SimulationContext):
    context.spawn(chaos_monkey(context))
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(worker_task(context, order, task_id))
        task_id += 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(until=40.0)

Save it as preemptive_breakdowns.py and run python preemptive_breakdowns.py. It runs for 40 seconds in real time (factor=1.0) and prints each event.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
• on_printer holds the process of the order being labelled, so the breakdown process knows what to interrupt.
  • worker_task publishes each event with the order's key, orders-1 and so on, and with the task name label and its instance id. It takes the printer and labels for LABELLING seconds. When it is interrupted, it subtracts the time already worked, publishes interrupted with the cause, keeps the printer for REPAIR seconds, publishes printer_repaired and labels the rest. It publishes finished when the work is done.
  • chaos_monkey interrupts the order on the printer every JAM_EVERY seconds. An idle printer, or one under repair, has nothing to interrupt, so it does not jam. For jams at random times, replace the fixed wait with a random draw such as random.expovariate(1 / JAM_EVERY).
  • arrival_loop starts chaos_monkey once, then starts a worker_task for each arriving order.

docs.title: Python in a Blueprint: !python
docs.text:
A blueprint holds configuration as plain YAML, and the YAML Blueprints page covers that. When a simulation needs logic that YAML cannot express, the file can reference a Python object with !python module.attribute in place of a value. This guide covers when to use it, how a reference is found, what each field receives and the security note, and ends with the OML hot rolling twin as a worked case.

The advanced Postgres example is a complete blueprint with one Python process. Every file on this page is in the repository under docs/snippets/.

docs.title: When to Use It
docs.text:
Use !python when a blueprint needs one of these:

  • Field values with logic. Random or weighted choices, fields derived from other fields and state carried from one event to the next are a payload function or a process.
  • More than a task can describe. A task that holds several resources at once, or a breakdown that interrupts work in progress, is a process. Routing (next), priorities (priority and queue: priority) and stores and containers are plain YAML.
  • Readings other than the built-in statistics. stats: minimal publishes resource, store and container readings, a container's level among them. Use a telemetry function to publish variables and derived metrics.
  • Routing over several destinations, and serializers. A router or an Avro serializer is a Python object.
  • Setup a connector does not do itself, such as topics that only a router knows about.
  • A connector from another package.

A setting that is a value needs no Python. Environment variables, relative times, when: history and when: live, filesystem and catalog mappings, Iceberg schemas and Postgres tables are all plain YAML, as YAML Format lists. A value can still come from a module when another program already defines it, as the hot rolling twin below reads its broker address from src/config.py.

docs.title: How a Reference Is Resolved
docs.text:
!python module.attribute imports module and returns its attribute. The reference can name anything: a function, a class, a dictionary or a constant.

The longest prefix that is a module is imported, and the rest is read as attributes, so pkg.module.func and module.Class.attribute both work. The folder of the YAML file is added to the front of sys.path, unless it is already on it, before anything is resolved, so a module beside the blueprint is found from any working directory. Other modules are found on the normal sys.path, which includes installed packages. ${VAR} is replaced inside a reference too, so !python ${LOGIC}.ticker picks the module from the environment.

Every reference is resolved and checked when the file is loaded, so a wrong reference fails before the run starts, with the file and line.

Field Must be Called as processes[].function a generator function function(context, **kwargs) when the run starts tasks.<name>.payload a callable, or a mapping payload(task_id, context) once per finished task telemetry[].function a callable function(context) every interval egress[].when a callable, or history or live when(record), True to send the record to that sink ingress[].type, egress[].type a class, or a short name type(**config) while the blueprint is built run.before[] a callable before() once, at the start of run() any value under config, simulation or run.until whatever that argument takes not called

docs.title: Processes, Payloads and kwargs
docs.text:
This blueprint keeps the shop in YAML and moves three pieces of logic into Python: a payload that picks each order's delivery, a breaks process with arguments, and a predicate that keeps telemetry off the terminal:

docs/snippets/yaml/hybrid.yaml
# The shop with its logic in Python. YAML keeps the blueprint and the
# experiment; shop_logic.py beside this file holds what YAML cannot express.
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0
  random_seed: 1

egress:
  - type: Console
    # Only events reach the terminal; telemetry is dropped.
    when: !python shop_logic.events_only

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 3}

services:
  packing: {dist: normal, mean: 4.0, std: 1.0}

arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.2, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    # Called as choose_delivery(task_id, context) for every packed order.
    payload: !python shop_logic.choose_delivery

processes:
  # Called as breaks(context, resource="packers", every=50, duration=5).
  - function: !python shop_logic.breaks
    kwargs: {resource: packers, every: 50, duration: 5}

scenario:
  - {at: 1 min, path: Shop.arrival.orders.rate, value: 0.4}

run:
  until: 3 min
docs/snippets/yaml/shop_logic.py
"""Python for the blueprints beside it: a payload, a process with arguments, a
predicate and a custom reading."""


def choose_delivery(task_id: int, context):
    """Picks each order's delivery from the shared generator, so a seed repeats it."""
    delivery = "standard" if context.sampler.rng.random() < 0.9 else "express"
    return {"status": "finished", "order_id": task_id, "delivery": delivery}


def breaks(context, resource: str, every: float, duration: float):
    """Waits `every` seconds, then takes every packer off for a break of `duration`."""
    path = f"{context.sim_id}.resources.{resource}.current_cap"
    registry = context.env.registry
    while True:
        yield context.env.timeout(every)
        normal = registry.get(path).value
        registry.update(path, 0)
        context.env.publish_event(f"{resource}-break", {"status": "down"})
        yield context.env.timeout(duration)
        registry.update(path, normal)
        context.env.publish_event(f"{resource}-break", {"status": "up"})


def events_only(record: dict) -> bool:
    """Egress predicate: keeps events and drops telemetry."""
    return record["stream_type"] == "event"


def packers_report(context):
    """A custom reading: orders waiting per packer, and the live arrival rate."""
    packers = context.get_resource("packers")
    waiting = len(packers.queue.items)
    context.publish("waiting_per_packer", waiting / max(packers.capacity, 1))
    rate = context.env.registry.get(f"{context.sim_id}.arrival.orders.rate").value
    context.publish("arrival_rate", rate)  # as Shop.arrival_rate

What each reference receives:

  • payload is called as choose_delivery(task_id, context) for every packed order. It draws from context.sampler, the generator seeded by random_seed, so the deliveries repeat with the seed.
  • processes entries are called as function(context, **kwargs) when the run starts. kwargs is how one function serves several resources.
  • when is called with every record and returns True to send it to that sink.

The run shows both:

[EVT] {'sim_ts': 5.369, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'status': 'finished', 'order_id': 0, 'delivery': 'standard'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 50.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'packers-break', 'task': None, 'instance': None, 'value': {'status': 'down'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 55.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'packers-break', 'task': None, 'instance': None, 'value': {'status': 'up'}}

A process is written either as a bare reference, - !python module.func, which is called as func(context), or as a mapping with function and kwargs, which is called as func(context, **kwargs). kwargs is what lets a blueprint start a process whose signature is not (context). When the signature differs more, write a small adapter: a generator function that takes the context, picks out what the process needs, and hands over with yield from.

docs/snippets/hot_rolling/hot_rolling_adapter.py:arrivals
def arrivals(context, product):
    yield from arrival_process(
        context.env,
        product,
        VARIABLE_PASSES,
        MAX_PASSES,
        context.sampler,
        context.get_resource(f"mill_{product}"),
    )

A process must be a generator function, one that contains yield. The check runs when the file is loaded and looks only at the function, so an adapter that returns a generator instead of yielding from one is rejected. Write adapters with yield from.

docs.title: Routers, Serializers and Connector Classes
docs.text:
A router replaces the default destination of every record. path_router on Parquet and JSONL and table_router on Iceberg each take a function that receives a record and returns its destination, or None to drop it. topic_router on Kafka must always return a topic. To drop records before Kafka, give the sink a when predicate. With a router, records are written as the router leaves them, so flattening events and dropping telemetry become the router's job. Kafka also leaves topic creation to the caller, because only the router knows which topics it uses. The hot rolling twin below sends every record to one of four topics with topic_router: !python routing.custom_topic_router.

A serializer is an object, so it is built in a module and referenced. KafkaEgress takes default_serializer and topic_serializers, for example default_serializer: !python serializers.AVRO, where serializers.py builds a ConfluentAvroSerializer with the registry URL and the schema.

A connector from another package is referenced by class: type: !python my_package.MyEgress. Its config is passed to the constructor, as for a built-in one.

docs.title: Setup with run.before
docs.text:
run.before lists functions called with no arguments, once, at the start of run(). Connectors already create what they write to when they can: Kafka its event and telemetry topics, Postgres the tables under tables, and Parquet and JSONL their folders. run.before is for anything else, such as the five topics the hot rolling twin below creates for its router.

Put such setup in a function rather than at the top of the module. The module is imported when the file is loaded, so its top-level code runs even when the file is loaded and never run.

docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:before
run:
  until: 1 hour
  before:
    - !python routing_logic.make_output_folder

The module beside the blueprint holds the setup function, and the path_router its Jsonl sink uses:

docs/snippets/yaml_build/routing_logic.py
"""Python for docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml: a router and a setup step."""

import os


def daily_path(record: dict):
    """Writes each event under its day; drops telemetry by returning None."""
    if record["stream_type"] != "event":
        return None
    return f"events/day={record['timestamp'][:10]}/events.jsonl"


def make_output_folder() -> None:
    """Called once by run.before, when the run starts, not when the file is loaded."""
    os.makedirs("events", exist_ok=True)

docs.title: Worked Case: Lift the OML Hot Rolling Twin
docs.text:
The OML hot rolling digital twin is a steel mill written with the low-level API. Its generator.py builds a SimParameter with three arrivals, three services, three resources, three containers and three variables, wires Kafka in both directions with a topic router, and starts the processes in sim_logic.py. Those processes take (env, sampler, resource, ...), not a context, and sim_logic.py runs to 262 lines of multi-stage routing, wear and physics.

The configuration moves to YAML. The processes keep their logic, and a small adapter changes only how they are called.

docs/snippets/hot_rolling/hot_rolling.yaml
# The OML hot rolling digital twin as a blueprint. The parameters and the Kafka
# wiring that generator.py builds in Python are declared here. The processes stay
# in sim_logic.py, and hot_rolling_adapter.py beside this file adapts them.
#
# Place this file and the adapter in sim_control/, then run from there:
#   desflow run hot_rolling.yaml
simulation:
  sim_id: HotRolling
  factor: 1.0
  random_seed: 42

ingress:
  # Control commands from the dashboard.
  - type: Kafka
    config:
      bootstrap_servers: !python src.config.KAFKA_BROKER
      topic: !python src.config.TOPIC_CONTROL_INGRESS

egress:
  # One producer; the router picks one of four topics for every record.
  - type: Kafka
    config:
      bootstrap_servers: !python src.config.KAFKA_BROKER
      topic_router: !python routing.custom_topic_router

arrivals:
  structural: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.2}
  microalloyed: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.15}
  high_alloy: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.1}

services:
  pass_roughing: {dist: normal, mean: 2.0, std: 0.2}
  pass_intermediate: {dist: normal, mean: 4.5, std: 0.5}
  pass_finishing: {dist: normal, mean: 8.0, std: 1.2}

resources:
  mill_structural: {current_cap: 4, max_cap: 10}
  mill_microalloyed: {current_cap: 4, max_cap: 10}
  mill_high_alloy: {current_cap: 4, max_cap: 10}

containers:
  # The wear is the level; current_cap is the most wear a roll can have
  wear_structural: {current_cap: 100.0, max_cap: 100.0, level: 0.001}
  wear_microalloyed: {current_cap: 100.0, max_cap: 100.0, level: 0.001}
  wear_high_alloy: {current_cap: 100.0, max_cap: 100.0, level: 0.001}

variables:
  velocity_structural: {type: abrupt, value: 0.0}
  velocity_microalloyed: {type: abrupt, value: 0.0}
  velocity_high_alloy: {type: abrupt, value: 0.0}

processes:
  # Started in the order generator.py starts them.
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.drift
    kwargs: {product_lines: [structural, microalloyed, high_alloy]}
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.monitor
    kwargs: {product_lines: [structural, microalloyed, high_alloy]}
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.primer
    kwargs: {product: structural}
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.arrivals
    kwargs: {product: structural}
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.primer
    kwargs: {product: microalloyed}
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.arrivals
    kwargs: {product: microalloyed}
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.primer
    kwargs: {product: high_alloy}
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.arrivals
    kwargs: {product: high_alloy}

# A reproducible drift experiment, which the dashboard otherwise drives by hand:
# gradual wear on the structural line from 10 minutes.
scenario:
  - at: 10 min
    path: HotRolling.variables.velocity_structural
    value: {type: gradual, value: 0.5, freq: 1}

run:
  before:
    - !python hot_rolling_adapter.create_topics
docs/snippets/hot_rolling/hot_rolling_adapter.py
"""Adapts the hot rolling processes to the calls a blueprint makes.

A blueprint calls every process as `function(context, **kwargs)`. The processes in
sim_logic.py take `(env, sampler, resource, ...)` instead, so each function here
takes the context, picks out what the process needs, and hands over with
`yield from`. Only the wear paths in sim_logic.py change, from `current_cap` to
`level`.
"""

import time
import uuid

from desflow import KafkaAdminConnector
from generator import telemetry_monitor
from sim_logic import arrival_process, drift_engine, roll_slab
from src.config import (
    KAFKA_BROKER,
    TOPIC_CONTROL_INGRESS,
    TOPIC_GROUND_TRUTH,
    TOPIC_LIFECYCLE,
    TOPIC_PREDICTION_REQUESTS,
    TOPIC_TELEMETRY,
)

# The command-line options of generator.py, fixed here.
VARIABLE_PASSES = False
MAX_PASSES = 5


def drift(context, product_lines):
    yield from drift_engine(context.env, product_lines)


def monitor(context, product_lines):
    yield from telemetry_monitor(context.env, product_lines)


def primer(context, product):
    """Rolls a first slab, so the mill does not start dry."""
    yield from roll_slab(
        context.env,
        uuid.uuid4().hex[:8].upper(),
        product,
        VARIABLE_PASSES,
        MAX_PASSES,
        context.sampler,
        context.get_resource(f"mill_{product}"),
    )


def arrivals(context, product):
    yield from arrival_process(
        context.env,
        product,
        VARIABLE_PASSES,
        MAX_PASSES,
        context.sampler,
        context.get_resource(f"mill_{product}"),
    )


def create_topics():
    """Creates the five topics generator.py creates before it starts."""
    KafkaAdminConnector(bootstrap_servers=KAFKA_BROKER).create_topics(
        topics_config=[
            {"name": TOPIC_CONTROL_INGRESS, "partitions": 1},
            {"name": TOPIC_TELEMETRY, "partitions": 1},
            {"name": TOPIC_LIFECYCLE, "partitions": 1},
            {"name": TOPIC_PREDICTION_REQUESTS, "partitions": 3},
            {"name": TOPIC_GROUND_TRUTH, "partitions": 3},
        ]
    )
    time.sleep(2)

What moved. The whole SimParameter, both Kafka connectors with the custom topic router, the seed, the factor and the topic creation. The broker address and the topic names stay in src/config.py, and the blueprint references them. containers and variables carry the wear levels and drift velocities the processes read and write.

What stayed. drift_engine, arrival_process, roll_slab and telemetry_monitor, with one change: they read and write the wear at HotRolling.containers.wear_<grade>.current_cap, and a container's current_cap is now its capacity, so those paths in sim_logic.py and dashboard.py become .level. The adapter is one generator function per process. Each takes the context, picks out the environment, the sampler and the mill resource, and hands over with yield from. The primer slab and the arrival loop are separate entries, so they start in the order generator.py starts them.

What is new. The scenario turns on gradual wear on the structural line at ten minutes. The twin's dashboard does this by hand over Kafka. As a scenario it repeats exactly, and it can still be combined with the dashboard, because both write to the same registry.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A reference that cannot be resolved stops the load with its line:

Error: err.yaml:6: !python shop_logic.missing: 'shop_logic' has no attribute 'missing'

A module that exists but fails on one of its own imports is reported with that error, rather than as a missing module.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Loading a blueprint runs the imports it names. !python imports modules, and importing a module runs its top-level code. A blueprint is therefore as trusted as a Python script: load only files you would run as code, in a local or trusted CI workflow.

Every other node is constructed by yaml.SafeLoader, and the tag is registered on a subclass of it, so yaml.safe_load elsewhere in the process is unaffected. Only !python is added to YAML. Every other tag, such as !!python/object, is rejected as yaml.safe_load rejects it.

docs.title: Distributions
docs.text:
Every distribution family desflow can draw from, generated from the registry of distributions in the code. Arrivals and Services explains how a draw works, and how each family is seeded and changed live.

Each family lists its parameters, the rules they must follow, and the registry path of each parameter that can change during a run. The mean, variance and value with no random generator are computed by the family's own functions for the example given. In a blueprint, a time-valued parameter (mean, std, low, mode, high, scale, value, values, edges) also takes a duration such as 5 min.

Family Parameters Live paths exponential rate .rate normal mean, std .mean, .std lognormal mean, std .mean, .std truncated_normal mean, std, low .mean, .std, .low constant value .value uniform low, high .low, .high triangular low, mode, high .low, .mode, .high gamma shape, scale .shape, .scale weibull shape, scale .shape, .scale empirical values, weights, edges, counts none

docs.title: exponential
docs.text:
Gaps between independent arrivals; the memoryless distribution.

dist exponential Parameters rate Defaults none Rules rate > 0, in events per second Registry paths <sim_id>.service.<name>.rate (and .arrival. for an arrival) Uses a random number yes

For the example {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5}: mean 2, variance 4, and with no random generator every draw is 2.

docs.title: normal
docs.text:
Symmetric times around a mean. Draws below 0.00001 s (min_delay) are raised to it, which raises the mean; truncated_normal avoids that.

dist normal Parameters mean, std Defaults std 0 Rules std >= 0; a std of 0 gives the mean every time Registry paths <sim_id>.service.<name>.mean, <sim_id>.service.<name>.std (and .arrival. for an arrival) Uses a random number yes

For the example {dist: normal, mean: 3.0, std: 0.5}: mean 3, variance 0.25, and with no random generator every draw is 3.

docs.title: lognormal
docs.text:
Positive times with a long right tail, given by their mean and std.

dist lognormal Parameters mean, std Defaults std 0 Rules mean > 0, std >= 0 Registry paths <sim_id>.service.<name>.mean, <sim_id>.service.<name>.std (and .arrival. for an arrival) Uses a random number yes

For the example {dist: lognormal, mean: 4.0, std: 3.0}: mean 4, variance 9, and with no random generator every draw is 4.

docs.title: truncated_normal
docs.text:
A normal that draws again below low instead of clamping.

dist truncated_normal Parameters mean, std, low Defaults std 0, low 0 Rules std >= 0; low is 0 when not given; with std 0, mean >= low Registry paths <sim_id>.service.<name>.mean, <sim_id>.service.<name>.std, <sim_id>.service.<name>.low (and .arrival. for an arrival) Uses a random number yes

For the example {dist: truncated_normal, mean: 1.0, std: 1.0, low: 0.0}: mean 1.288, variance 0.6297, and with no random generator every draw is 1.

docs.title: constant
docs.text:
The same time every draw, such as a conveyor or a set-up.

dist constant Parameters value Defaults none Rules value >= 0 Registry paths <sim_id>.service.<name>.value (and .arrival. for an arrival) Uses a random number no

For the example {dist: constant, value: 1.5}: mean 1.5, variance 0, and with no random generator every draw is 1.5.

docs.title: uniform
docs.text:
Every time between low and high equally likely.

dist uniform Parameters low, high Defaults none Rules low < high Registry paths <sim_id>.service.<name>.low, <sim_id>.service.<name>.high (and .arrival. for an arrival) Uses a random number yes

For the example {dist: uniform, low: 1.0, high: 2.0}: mean 1.5, variance 0.08333, and with no random generator every draw is 1.5.

docs.title: triangular
docs.text:
An expert's estimate: the shortest, the most likely and the longest time.

dist triangular Parameters low, mode, high Defaults none Rules low <= mode <= high, low < high Registry paths <sim_id>.service.<name>.low, <sim_id>.service.<name>.mode, <sim_id>.service.<name>.high (and .arrival. for an arrival) Uses a random number yes

For the example {dist: triangular, low: 1.0, mode: 1.25, high: 2.25}: mean 1.5, variance 0.07292, and with no random generator every draw is 1.5.

docs.title: gamma
docs.text:
Times less variable than exponential. A whole-number shape is the Erlang distribution: that many exponential steps in a row.

dist gamma Parameters shape, scale Defaults none Rules shape > 0, scale > 0; mean = shape * scale Registry paths <sim_id>.service.<name>.shape, <sim_id>.service.<name>.scale (and .arrival. for an arrival) Uses a random number yes

For the example {dist: gamma, shape: 9.0, scale: 0.1667}: mean 1.5, variance 0.2501, and with no random generator every draw is 1.5.

docs.title: weibull
docs.text:
Time to failure: a shape below 1 fails early, above 1 wears out.

dist weibull Parameters shape, scale Defaults none Rules shape > 0, scale > 0 Registry paths <sim_id>.service.<name>.shape, <sim_id>.service.<name>.scale (and .arrival. for an arrival) Uses a random number yes

For the example {dist: weibull, shape: 1.5, scale: 3600.0}: mean 3250, variance 4.869e+06, and with no random generator every draw is 3250.

docs.title: empirical
docs.text:
Times taken from real data: listed values with optional weights, or a histogram of edges and counts. Taken at load; they do not change live.

dist empirical Parameters values, weights, edges, counts Defaults none Rules values, or edges and counts; one weight per value and one count per bin, each 0 or more and adding up to more than 0; edges increasing Registry paths none: the lists are taken at load Uses a random number yes

For the example {dist: empirical, values: [1.2, 1.5, 1.5, 2.1, 3.0]}: mean 1.86, variance 0.4104, and with no random generator every draw is 1.86.

docs.title: Records and Telemetry
docs.text:
Everything a simulation publishes is a record of one of three kinds: a telemetry record for a single value, an event record for something that happened to an entity, and a label record for the ground truth of a scenario step. The records have the shape of the TelemetryPayload, EventPayload and LabelPayload models, and they are the same whichever way the simulation was written.

All three share stream_type, sim_ts and timestamp. Telemetry names its value in path_id; an event names its entity in key and its task in task and instance; a label carries what a step changed:

docs.title: Record Shape
docs.text:
Every sink, router and when predicate receives records as plain dictionaries, with these keys in this order:

Field Telemetry Event Label stream_type "telemetry" "event" "label" sim_ts simulation seconds simulation seconds simulation seconds timestamp logical time logical time logical time path_id the name of the value key the entity's key, such as orders-1 task the task's name, or None instance the task's instance id, or None path the registry path the step changed, or None old, new the value before and after, or None label the step's record mapping value a single value the event's value

As ConsoleEgress prints them, a statistic and the three events of one task:

[TEL] {'sim_ts': 10.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.in_use', 'value': 0}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 3.672, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'queued'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 3.672, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'started'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 5.369, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_packed'}}

And two labels, as a JSON Lines sink writes them:

{"stream_type":"label","sim_ts":30.0,"timestamp":"...","path":"Shop.arrival.orders.rate","old":0.5,"new":1.5,"label":{"fault":"order_surge","cause":"flash sale"}}
{"stream_type":"label","sim_ts":45.0,"timestamp":"...","path":null,"old":null,"new":null,"label":{"fault":"label_printer_offline"}}

sim_ts is simulation seconds. timestamp is logical_start_time plus sim_ts, as an ISO string with milliseconds, with no time zone unless logical_start_time has one.

docs.title: Field Values
docs.text:
• sim_ts is rounded to three decimal places and is always a float, so simulation time 0 is 0.0.
  • key and path_id are strings. bytes and bytearray are decoded to strings; any other type, such as an int, raises a Pydantic ValidationError at the call.
  • value, old, new and label are converted to plain JSON values before any sink sees them. A Pydantic V2 model becomes a dictionary, a datetime an ISO string, and a NaN or an infinity None, in a model at any depth as in a plain dictionary.
docs/snippets/pages/records.py:values
class Reading(BaseModel):
    sensor: str
    celsius: float
    taken_at: datetime


def readings(context: SimulationContext):
    while True:
        yield context.env.timeout(30.0)
        reading = Reading(
            sensor="spindle", celsius=float("nan"), taken_at=datetime.now()
        )
        # The model becomes a dict, taken_at an ISO string, and NaN becomes None
        context.env.publish_event("sensor-spindle", reading)

docs.title: Task Events
docs.text:
@app.task and a YAML task publish three events for each run, all with the entity's key, the task's name and its instance id:

Event value queued {"path_id": "<sim_id>.service.<service>", "status": "queued"} started {"path_id": "<sim_id>.service.<service>", "status": "started"} finished exactly what the task returns, or the YAML payload

A task with no service has {"status": ...} without path_id. A timed step, with a service and no resource, publishes no queued. A task with no service, resource or get publishes only the finished event, as soon as it starts. The key is the arrival's name and a counter from 1, such as orders-1, on every event of every task the entity passes through; Task Flow describes it. A low-level process publishes whatever it passes to env.publish_event(key, value, task=..., instance=...).

docs.title: Telemetry Names
docs.text:
Published by path_id the built-in statistics <sim_id>.stats.<kind>.<name>.<statistic>, such as Shop.stats.resources.packers.in_use; Reference, Statistics lists every name context.publish(name, value) and a YAML telemetry function <sim_id>.<name> env.publish_telemetry(path_id, value) path_id, as given the lag monitor system.simulation.lag_seconds, once per simulation second docs/snippets/pages/records.py:telemetry
@app.telemetry_loop(interval=10.0)
def report(context: SimulationContext):
    # path_id is Shop.packers_free: the sim_id is added in front
    packers = context.get_resource("packers")
    context.publish("packers_free", packers.capacity - packers.in_use)
docs/snippets/pages/records.py:low-level
env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)
env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])
env.publish_telemetry("plant.power_kw", 412.5)  # path_id exactly as given
# key, task, instance and value as given; task and instance are optional
env.publish_event("orders-17", {"status": "shipped"}, task="ship", instance=16)
# A ground-truth label, which only a when: labels sink receives
env.publish_label({"fault": "slow_packing"}, path="Shop.service.packing.scale")

docs.title: What Each Sink Writes
docs.text:
Every sink receives the events and telemetry above, and a when: labels sink receives the labels instead. What each writes differs:

Sink Writes ConsoleEgress one log line per record, [TEL], [EVT] or [LBL] followed by the record without stream_type KafkaEgress the record as JSON, without stream_type unless include_stream_type=True; the message key is path_id for telemetry and key for an event. A label goes to event_topic with no key RedisEgress the record as JSON in one payload field, with any __stream__ key removed ParquetStorageEgress, JsonlStorageEgress, IcebergStorageEgress without a router, one flat row per event or label, with an event's value mapping unpacked into columns, and no telemetry; with a router, each record as the router leaves it PostgresEgress an event or telemetry record whose value is a mapping, with sim_ts, timestamp, key as event_id, task and instance, or path_id, added to it, as Egress describes; a label as the columns sim_ts, timestamp, path, old, new and label, the last three as JSON text

docs.title: Statistic Names
docs.text: Every name the built-in statistics publish, at each level, generated by running the statistics in the code. Statistics explains the levels and how each value is computed. Each level publishes the names of the levels before it, and the new ones listed under it. <sim_id> is the simulation's id, <name> a resource, store or container, <task> a task, and <arrival> the arrival that started a flow's entities.

docs.title: none
docs.text: Publishes nothing: the statistics are off.

docs.title: minimal
docs.text: Name Measures <sim_id>.stats.resources.<name>.capacity units now <sim_id>.stats.resources.<name>.in_use units held by tasks; above capacity after a drop, until they finish <sim_id>.stats.resources.<name>.queue_length requests waiting now <sim_id>.stats.resources.<name>.utilization in_use as a percentage of capacity, now <sim_id>.stats.stores.<name>.capacity items it can hold now <sim_id>.stats.stores.<name>.level items held now <sim_id>.stats.stores.<name>.getters_waiting tasks waiting to get an item <sim_id>.stats.stores.<name>.putters_waiting tasks waiting to put an item <sim_id>.stats.containers.<name>.capacity largest amount, now <sim_id>.stats.containers.<name>.level amount held now <sim_id>.stats.containers.<name>.getters_waiting tasks waiting to take an amount <sim_id>.stats.containers.<name>.putters_waiting tasks waiting to add an amount

docs.title: basic
docs.text: Name Measures <sim_id>.stats.resources.<name>.utilization_avg utilisation averaged over time, in percent <sim_id>.stats.resources.<name>.queue_length_avg requests waiting, averaged over time <sim_id>.stats.stores.<name>.level_avg items held, averaged over time <sim_id>.stats.containers.<name>.level_avg amount held, averaged over time <sim_id>.stats.tasks.<task>.finished instances finished so far <sim_id>.stats.flows.<arrival>.finished entities that left the model, by the arrival that started them

docs.title: typical
docs.text: Name Measures <sim_id>.stats.tasks.<task>.wait_mean mean time from queued to started <sim_id>.stats.tasks.<task>.wait_max longest time from queued to started <sim_id>.stats.tasks.<task>.service_mean mean time from started to finished <sim_id>.stats.tasks.<task>.service_max longest time from started to finished

docs.title: all
docs.text: Name Measures <sim_id>.stats.tasks.<task>.wait_p50 median wait <sim_id>.stats.tasks.<task>.wait_p95 the wait 95% of instances stay under <sim_id>.stats.tasks.<task>.wait_p99 the wait 99% of instances stay under <sim_id>.stats.tasks.<task>.service_p50 median service time <sim_id>.stats.tasks.<task>.service_p95 the service time 95% of instances stay under <sim_id>.stats.tasks.<task>.service_p99 the service time 99% of instances stay under

docs.title: YAML Format
docs.text:
Every key a blueprint accepts, section by section. YAML Blueprints describes how a file is read and where an error points, and each User Guide page shows its keys in use.

Every section is optional except simulation. Unknown keys are refused, so a misspelt key is reported with its line rather than ignored. A time is seconds or a duration such as 10 min, and an instant is now, a signed duration such as -1d, or an ISO datetime. ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} read environment variables anywhere in the file.

Each section becomes one builder call:

A blueprint with logic in Python beside it, which the sections below refer to:

docs/snippets/yaml/hybrid.yaml
# The shop with its logic in Python. YAML keeps the blueprint and the
# experiment; shop_logic.py beside this file holds what YAML cannot express.
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0
  random_seed: 1

egress:
  - type: Console
    # Only events reach the terminal; telemetry is dropped.
    when: !python shop_logic.events_only

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 3}

services:
  packing: {dist: normal, mean: 4.0, std: 1.0}

arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.2, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    # Called as choose_delivery(task_id, context) for every packed order.
    payload: !python shop_logic.choose_delivery

processes:
  # Called as breaks(context, resource="packers", every=50, duration=5).
  - function: !python shop_logic.breaks
    kwargs: {resource: packers, every: 50, duration: 5}

scenario:
  - {at: 1 min, path: Shop.arrival.orders.rate, value: 0.4}

run:
  until: 3 min

docs.title: simulation
docs.text:
The arguments of SimulationContext. Time and Pacing describes the clock.

Key Value sim_id required; the first part of every registry path and statistic name factor 1.0 follows the wall clock, 0 does not wait; 1.0 by default random_seed a whole number; without one, the run draws a seed and logs it logical_start_time the instant simulation time 0 maps to; the load time by default go_live_at the instant from which the run is paced in real time warmup a time, 0 or more, before which no sink receives a record and at which the statistics restart

docs.title: resources, stores and containers
docs.text:
name: {...} entries. Resources and Stores and Containers describe them.

Section Keys resources current_cap and max_cap, whole numbers; queue: fifo (the default), lifo or priority stores current_cap and max_cap, whole numbers of items containers current_cap and max_cap, the largest amount; level, the amount at the start, 0 by default

A store and a container cannot share a name.

docs.title: variables
docs.text: name: value entries, any YAML value, each at the registry path <sim_id>.variables.<name>. Live Parameters describes them.

docs.title: services and arrivals
docs.text:
name: {dist, ...} entries: a distribution family and the parameters it takes. Time-valued parameters take durations, and rate is per second. Arrivals and Services shows each family, and Reference, Distributions lists their parameters and rules.

An arrival also takes:

Key Value spawn the task each arrival starts attributes a mapping each new entity starts with, read as attr.<name>

docs.title: tasks
docs.text:
name: {...} entries, each built with @app.task. Tasks and Processes and Task Flow describe them.

Key Value service the service whose time the task takes; needed with a resource resource the resource the task holds while it works payload required: the finished event's value, a mapping, or a !python function called as function(task_id, context) id_field adds the task id to a mapping payload under this key attributes a list of entity attributes added to a mapping payload priority a number or an expression such as attr.tier, for a resource with queue: priority get {container: name, amount: ...} or {store: name}: taken after the resource, before the work put the same form: added after the work; a store receives the payload next a task name; {when: [{condition, task}, ...], default: task}; or {weights: {task: number, ...}} set a mapping applied to the entity's attributes when the task finishes

An amount is a number or an expression, 1 when left out. A task with a service and no resource is a timed step; one with neither, and no get, takes no time.

docs.title: processes
docs.text: A list of !python generator functions, each written as {function: ..., kwargs: {...}} or as the bare reference, started as function(context, **kwargs); Python in a Blueprint shows them.

docs.title: telemetry
docs.text:
A list of custom readings, each {interval, function}: every interval simulation seconds, greater than 0, function(context) is called and publishes with context.publish. The built-in readings of resources, stores and containers come from stats instead.

docs/snippets/yaml/telemetry.yaml:telemetry
telemetry:
  # Every 5 simulation seconds, calls packers_report(context), which publishes
  # Shop.waiting_per_packer and Shop.arrival_rate with context.publish
  - interval: 5
    function: !python shop_logic.packers_report

docs.title: stats
docs.text: The built-in statistics, as a level, stats: basic, or as a mapping, stats: {level: all, interval: 1 min}. The level is none, minimal, basic, typical or all, and the interval, 10 seconds by default, is a time greater than 0. Statistics describes them.

docs.title: scenario
docs.text:
A list of steps, applied in time order on the simulation clock:

Key Value at the time of the step path a registry path, checked when the file loads; needs a value value the new value, which must convert to the type the path holds record a mapping, published as a ground-truth label to the when: labels sinks

A step needs a path and value, a record, or both. Live Parameters shows scenarios and labels.

docs.title: ingress and egress
docs.text:
Lists of connectors, each with a type and a config of the constructor's keyword arguments. type is one of the short names below, or a !python class from another package. A connector's module is imported only when a blueprint names it, so a blueprint that uses Kafka does not need the PostgreSQL driver; a missing package stops the load with its line and the pip install command, except Parquet and JSON Lines, which import PyArrow when they start writing.

Direction type Class Extra ingress Local LocalIngress none ingress Kafka KafkaIngress kafka ingress Postgres PostgresIngress postgres ingress Redis RedisIngress redis egress Console ConsoleEgress none egress Kafka KafkaEgress kafka egress Parquet ParquetStorageEgress parquet egress Jsonl JsonlStorageEgress parquet egress Iceberg IcebergStorageEgress iceberg egress Postgres PostgresEgress postgres egress Redis RedisEgress redis

An egress entry also takes when: history or live, both needing simulation.go_live_at, labels, or a !python function of one record; and batch_size and flush_interval, both greater than 0. Ingress and Egress describe them.

Settings that the Python API takes as objects are plain values:

type Setting Plain value Kafka topics Without a topic_router, event_topic and telemetry_topic are created when the run starts, with one partition each, if they do not exist. Parquet, Jsonl filesystem A mapping. type is local (the default) or s3, and the other keys are passed to PyArrow's S3FileSystem, such as endpoint_override, access_key, secret_key and region. An endpoint_override starting with http:// sets the scheme. A key whose value is empty is left out. Parquet, Jsonl default_path Without a path_router, each event is written there as one flat row, with its value mapping unpacked into columns, and telemetry is left out. The folder is created on the first write. Iceberg catalog A mapping of PyIceberg catalog properties, such as type, uri, warehouse and s3.endpoint, passed to load_catalog on the first write. An optional name key names the catalog. Iceberg default_table, schemas Without a table_router, each event is written to default_table as one flat row. schemas maps a table to its columns, each with a type: string, int, long, float, double, boolean, timestamp, timestamptz, date or binary. Postgres tables Tables created when the run starts, if they do not exist. Each maps to columns, a mapping of column name to SQL type, and an optional primary_key. table_name defaults to the table when tables names one.

An ISO time string bound for a timestamp or date column of Iceberg or PostgreSQL is converted before the write.

docs.title: batching
docs.text: The arguments of with_batching, the defaults for every sink: batch_size and flush_interval, and optionally max_queued_batches and drain_stall_seconds, all greater than 0. Egress describes them.

docs.title: run
docs.text: Key Value until a time greater than 0; desflow run --until overrides it before a list of !python functions called with no arguments before the run, for setup such as creating topics

docs.title: Security
docs.text: A blueprint with no !python references is read entirely by yaml.SafeLoader, and loading it imports only the connector modules its type entries name. A file that references Python runs the imports it names, so it is as trusted as a Python script: run blueprints from people you would take a script from. Python in a Blueprint explains.

docs.title: Choosing Inputs
docs.text: Packing takes 1.5 seconds on average. So far the shop has said exactly that: a constant 1.5 seconds. Real packing times vary, and a model is only as good as the times it draws. This page asks: which distribution fits packing times?

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text:
A packing time chosen from evidence. The model simulates the busy hour with 3 packers from Queues and Capacity. It gets four candidates for packing, all with a mean of 1.5 seconds, and runs the hour with each:

  • constant: the mean alone, as the shop had it;
  • exponential: the usual choice when nothing is known;
  • triangular: an expert's estimate;
  • empirical: times measured at the packing bench.

docs.title: An Expert's Range
docs.text:
Choosing a distribution for an input is called input modelling. Often there is no data yet, but someone who knows the work can say how long it takes at least, usually and at most. A triangular distribution takes exactly those three numbers, low, mode and high, and all three are required:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/choosing_inputs.yaml:triangular
# An expert's estimate: at least 1 s, usually 1.25 s, at most 2.25 s
triangular: {dist: triangular, low: 1 s, mode: 1.25 s, high: 2.25 s}
docs/snippets/tutorials/choosing_inputs.py:triangular
# An expert's estimate: at least 1 s, usually 1.25 s, at most 2.25 s
app.add_service("triangular", dist="triangular", low=1, mode=1.25, high=2.25)
docs/snippets/tutorials/choosing_inputs_low_level.py:triangular
# An expert's estimate: at least 1 s, usually 1.25 s, at most 2.25 s
TRIANGULAR = DistributionConfig(dist="triangular", low=1, mode=1.25, high=2.25)

Its mean is (low + mode + high) ÷ 3 = (1 + 1.25 + 2.25) ÷ 3 = 1.5 seconds. In a blueprint every time-valued parameter takes a duration such as 1.25 s or 2 min; a plain number is seconds.

docs.title: Measured Times
docs.text:
When times can be measured, use them. An empirical distribution draws from a list of measured values, each equally likely (or with weights, one per value). These are 40 packing times timed at the bench, with a mean of 1.5 seconds:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/choosing_inputs.yaml:empirical
# 40 packing times measured at the bench, in seconds
empirical:
  dist: empirical
  values: [1.5, 2.5, 2.4, 1.2, 1.3, 1.2, 1.8, 1.4, 2.0, 0.7,
           2.7, 1.4, 1.9, 1.4, 1.3, 1.8, 2.0, 1.4, 1.4, 1.9,
           1.1, 0.8, 1.7, 1.1, 0.7, 1.1, 1.2, 0.9, 0.8, 1.5,
           2.1, 1.3, 1.1, 1.7, 1.9, 1.3, 1.8, 2.2, 1.4, 1.1]
docs/snippets/tutorials/choosing_inputs.py:empirical
# 40 packing times measured at the bench, in seconds
measured = [
    1.5, 2.5, 2.4, 1.2, 1.3, 1.2, 1.8, 1.4, 2.0, 0.7,
    2.7, 1.4, 1.9, 1.4, 1.3, 1.8, 2.0, 1.4, 1.4, 1.9,
    1.1, 0.8, 1.7, 1.1, 0.7, 1.1, 1.2, 0.9, 0.8, 1.5,
    2.1, 1.3, 1.1, 1.7, 1.9, 1.3, 1.8, 2.2, 1.4, 1.1,
]  # fmt: skip
app.add_service("empirical", dist="empirical", values=measured)
docs/snippets/tutorials/choosing_inputs_low_level.py:empirical
# 40 packing times measured at the bench, in seconds
MEASURED = [
    1.5, 2.5, 2.4, 1.2, 1.3, 1.2, 1.8, 1.4, 2.0, 0.7,
    2.7, 1.4, 1.9, 1.4, 1.3, 1.8, 2.0, 1.4, 1.4, 1.9,
    1.1, 0.8, 1.7, 1.1, 0.7, 1.1, 1.2, 0.9, 0.8, 1.5,
    2.1, 1.3, 1.1, 1.7, 1.9, 1.3, 1.8, 2.2, 1.4, 1.1,
]  # fmt: skip
EMPIRICAL = DistributionConfig(dist="empirical", values=MEASURED)

The values are taken when the model is loaded. A list is not one number, so an empirical distribution has no registry path and does not change while the run goes on; the other distributions have one path per parameter, such as Shop.service.triangular.mode.

docs.title: Same Mean, Different Waits
docs.text:
All four candidates have the same mean, so the packers are equally busy with each: utilisation 0.9. Run the hour with each, and read the mean wait from the statistics at the typical level, which Measuring a Run explains:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/choosing_inputs.yaml:compare
tasks:
  pack_order:
    # The candidate comes from the PACKING variable, empirical when it is not set
    service: ${PACKING:-empirical}
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

# The mean wait of pack_order, published at the end
stats: {level: typical, interval: 1 h}

for packing in constant triangular empirical exponential; do
  PACKING=$packing desflow run choosing_inputs.yaml 2>&1 | grep wait_mean
done
docs/snippets/tutorials/choosing_inputs.py:compare
# The task packs with the candidate; the mean wait is read at the end
@app.task(service_id=packing, resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

app.with_stats("typical", interval=3600)
docs/snippets/tutorials/choosing_inputs_low_level.py:compare
def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, packing, task_id):
    """One order, packed with the candidate called `packing`."""
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        service = env.registry.get_config(f"Shop.service.{packing}")
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(service))
    env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)

The Builder and Low-level scripts print one line per candidate; the YAML runs print the same numbers as the value of their wait_mean lines:

constant     mean wait  1.27 s
triangular   mean wait  1.28 s
empirical    mean wait  1.35 s
exponential  mean wait  2.37 s

A mean alone hides queues. With constant packing nobody holds a packer for long. With exponential packing a few orders take 4, 5 or 6 seconds, and everyone behind them waits: the mean wait almost doubles at the same utilisation.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
Which distribution fits packing times? The empirical distribution, because it is the measured times themselves. On the left, the shapes of the four candidates; on the right, the mean wait each gives in the busy hour:

With the empirical distribution the mean wait is 1.35 seconds. The constant mean gives 1.27 seconds, 6% too short, and the exponential guess gives 2.37 seconds, 75% too long. The expert's triangle is close to the constant, because its range is narrower than the measured one.

docs.title: Why It Works
docs.text: In the busy hour the mean wait is roughly proportional to the square of the spread of the gaps between orders plus the square of the spread of the packing times, each spread measured relative to its mean (Kingman's approximation). The gaps are the same in all four runs, so only the packing spread differs: none for constant, a little for triangular, more for the measured times, and as much as the mean itself for exponential. A family fitted to the measured times, such as a gamma with their mean and standard deviation, takes other parameters, a shape and a scale; Arrivals and Services gives the formulas that turn a mean and a standard deviation into them, and lists each distribution with its parameters and rules. Distributions gives the mean and variance of each family.

docs.title: Full Files
docs.text:
Full files YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/choosing_inputs.yaml

docs/snippets/tutorials/choosing_inputs.py
"""The Choosing Inputs tutorial: the busy hour with four candidate packing times.

Each candidate has a mean of 1.5 seconds. The script runs the busy hour once per
candidate, unpaced, and prints the mean wait of each run.
"""

from desflow import SimulationContext

CANDIDATES = ["constant", "triangular", "empirical", "exponential"]


def shop(packing: str) -> SimulationContext:
    """The busy hour with 3 packers, packing with the service called `packing`."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        .add_resource("packers", current_cap=3, max_cap=10)
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=1.8)
        # Four candidates for packing, each with a mean of 1.5 seconds
        .add_service("constant", dist="constant", value=1.5)
        .add_service("exponential", dist="exponential", rate=0.6667)  # 1 / 1.5 s
    )
    # An expert's estimate: at least 1 s, usually 1.25 s, at most 2.25 s
    app.add_service("triangular", dist="triangular", low=1, mode=1.25, high=2.25)
    # 40 packing times measured at the bench, in seconds
    measured = [
        1.5, 2.5, 2.4, 1.2, 1.3, 1.2, 1.8, 1.4, 2.0, 0.7,
        2.7, 1.4, 1.9, 1.4, 1.3, 1.8, 2.0, 1.4, 1.4, 1.9,
        1.1, 0.8, 1.7, 1.1, 0.7, 1.1, 1.2, 0.9, 0.8, 1.5,
        2.1, 1.3, 1.1, 1.7, 1.9, 1.3, 1.8, 2.2, 1.4, 1.1,
    ]  # fmt: skip
    app.add_service("empirical", dist="empirical", values=measured)

    # The task packs with the candidate; the mean wait is read at the end
    @app.task(service_id=packing, resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    app.with_stats("typical", interval=3600)

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_generator(context):
        task_id = 0
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
            task_id += 1

    return app


def mean_wait(packing: str) -> float:
    """Runs the busy hour with one candidate and returns the mean wait."""
    app = shop(packing)
    app.run(until="1 h")
    return app.env.stats.readings()["Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean"]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for packing in CANDIDATES:
        print(f"{packing:<12} mean wait {mean_wait(packing):5.2f} s")
