"""The Choosing Inputs tutorial: the busy hour with four candidate packing times.

Each candidate has a mean of 1.5 seconds. The script runs the busy hour once per
candidate, unpaced, and prints the mean wait of each run.
"""

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

CANDIDATES = ["constant", "triangular", "empirical", "exponential"]
# An expert's estimate: at least 1 s, usually 1.25 s, at most 2.25 s
TRIANGULAR = DistributionConfig(dist="triangular", low=1, mode=1.25, high=2.25)
# 40 packing times measured at the bench, in seconds
MEASURED = [
    1.5, 2.5, 2.4, 1.2, 1.3, 1.2, 1.8, 1.4, 2.0, 0.7,
    2.7, 1.4, 1.9, 1.4, 1.3, 1.8, 2.0, 1.4, 1.4, 1.9,
    1.1, 0.8, 1.7, 1.1, 0.7, 1.1, 1.2, 0.9, 0.8, 1.5,
    2.1, 1.3, 1.1, 1.7, 1.9, 1.3, 1.8, 2.2, 1.4, 1.1,
]  # fmt: skip
EMPIRICAL = DistributionConfig(dist="empirical", values=MEASURED)


def params() -> SimParameter:
    """The busy hour with 3 packers and the four candidates."""
    return SimParameter(
        sim_id="Shop",
        arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=1.8)},
        # Four candidates for packing, each with a mean of 1.5 seconds
        service={
            "constant": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5),
            "exponential": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.6667),
            "triangular": TRIANGULAR,
            "empirical": EMPIRICAL,
        },
        resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=3, max_cap=10)},
    )


def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, packing, task_id):
    """One order, packed with the candidate called `packing`."""
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        service = env.registry.get_config(f"Shop.service.{packing}")
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(service))
    env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers, packing):
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, packing, task_id))
        task_id += 1


def mean_wait(packing: str) -> float:
    """Runs the busy hour with one candidate and returns the mean wait."""
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(params())
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=3600)
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    env.process(order_generator(env, Sampler(seed=42), packers, packing))
    try:
        env.run(until=3600)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env.stats.readings()["Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean"]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for packing in CANDIDATES:
        print(f"{packing:<12} mean wait {mean_wait(packing):5.2f} s")

Next, Measuring a Run asks what else a run can tell you.

docs.title: First Simulation
docs.text:
This tutorial models a shop that receives and packs customer orders: one packer, orders arriving about every 2 seconds, and 1.5 seconds of packing per order. It answers one question: how long does an order wait with one packer? The following pages extend the same model, one idea per page.

Each step shows the code three ways, in tabs: a YAML blueprint, the Builder (SimulationContext) and the Low-level API (DynamicRealtimeEnvironment and SimPy processes). Choose the tab for your preferred API; all code tabs on the site switch to that API. The three build the same simulation and print the same records. Ways to Write explains how they relate.

Look at the order of the parts: orders arrive, wait in the packer queue, take the packer for 1.5 seconds, and send their records to the console. The arrival loop and the task read their values from the registry.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The core package includes the desflow command:

pip install desflow

docs.title: Describe the Shop
docs.text:
In discrete-event simulation (DES), an entity is a thing that moves through the model, here an order. A resource is what an entity needs and may have to wait for, here the packer. A service time is how long an entity holds the resource, and an arrival process sets when entities appear.

In desflow these are parameters of one simulation, named by a sim_id, here Shop: a resource called packers with one unit, a service called packing, and an arrival stream called orders.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/first_shop.yaml:shop
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 1.0  # 1 simulated second takes 1 real second
  random_seed: 42  # the same arrival times on every run

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 1}

services:
  # Every order takes exactly 1.5 seconds to pack
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5}

arrivals:
  # One order every 2 seconds on average; each arrival spawns pack_order
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5, spawn: pack_order}
docs/snippets/tutorials/first_shop.py:shop
app = (
    # 1 simulated second = 1 real second; a seed gives the same arrivals every run
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0, random_seed=42)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
    # Every order takes exactly 1.5 seconds to pack
    .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
    # One order every 2 seconds on average
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
)
docs/snippets/tutorials/first_shop_low_level.py:shop
PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=1)},
)
SEED = 42  # the same arrival times on every run

Packing is constant, so every order takes 1.5 seconds and only the arrivals are random. The gaps between orders are drawn from an exponential distribution with a rate of 0.5 orders per second. The seed makes those draws the same on every run, so your trace matches the one below; Randomness and Seeds explains it.

Each value gets a path in the registry, such as Shop.arrival.orders.rate or Shop.resources.packers.current_cap. A scenario or a message from outside changes a value through its path while the run continues; Live Parameters explains how.

docs.title: Say What an Order Does
docs.text:
In DES terms an order queues for the packer, seizes it when it is free, is delayed for the service time, and releases the packer. desflow calls this a task. It publishes three events: queued when the order asks for a packer, started when it gets one, and a finished event at the end, whose value is the task's payload.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/first_shop.yaml:order
tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    # The value of the finished event
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

spawn: pack_order on the arrival, in the step above, starts the task for every order.

docs/snippets/tutorials/first_shop.py:order
@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    # Requests a packer, waits the packing time, releases the packer.
    # The returned dictionary is the value of the finished event.
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        # Waits for the next arrival and returns the new order, keyed orders-1, ...
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
        task_id += 1

@app.task publishes the three events and handles the packer for you. The arrival loop waits for each arrival and starts one pack_order for the order it returns.

docs/snippets/tutorials/first_shop_low_level.py:order
def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id):
    """One order: wait for a packer, pack it, release the packer."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        service = env.registry.get_config(path_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(service))
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers):
    """Starts one pack_order for every arrival, keyed orders-1, orders-2, ..."""
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id))
        task_id += 1

These are SimPy constructs. pack_order is a process: a generator function that the environment runs, pausing at each yield until the event it yielded happens. env.timeout(...) is an event that happens after a delay, and packers.request() is an event that happens when a packer is free; leaving the with block releases it. env.process(...) starts a process. SimPy and desflow describes what desflow adds to them.

docs.title: Print the Records
docs.text:
A sink, called an egress, receives every record the simulation publishes. ConsoleEgress prints them; Egress lists the others.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/first_shop.yaml:records
egress:
  - type: Console
docs/snippets/tutorials/first_shop.py:records
app.add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
docs/snippets/tutorials/first_shop_low_level.py:records
SINKS = [ConsoleEgress()]  # passed to env.setup_egress in run below

Every event record carries the order's key, orders-1 for the first order, so all the events of one order can be found together. task names the task, and instance counts the task's runs from 0. Records and Telemetry describes every field.

docs.title: Run It
Result
docs.text:
How long does an order wait with one packer? It depends on how many orders are ahead of it, as the same records on a timeline show: each order waits (yellow) until the packer is free, then holds it for 1.5 seconds of packing (blue).

orders-1 finds the packer free, so its queued and started events have the same time. orders-2 is the first order that has to wait: it is queued at 2.696 and started at 4.052, when orders-1 finishes. It waits 1.356 seconds. orders-3 arrives while orders-2 is waiting and waits longer, 1.815 seconds, because two orders are ahead of it.

So with one packer, an order that arrives while the packer is busy waits until every order ahead of it has been packed. The wait depends on when orders happen to arrive, which is why the next pages measure it over many orders.

docs.title: Why It Works
docs.text: A discrete-event simulation keeps a list of future events, ordered by time. It takes the earliest one, moves the clock to its time, and runs what it triggers, which may add new events to the list: an arrival schedules the next arrival, and a start of packing schedules its end 1.5 seconds later. The trace above is that list, read in order. What Is DES? explains the event list in more detail.

docs.title: Full Files
docs.text:
Full files

The complete first shop, which the documentation tests run:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/first_shop.yaml
# The First Simulation tutorial: the shop as a blueprint.
# Run it with: desflow run first_shop.yaml
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 1.0  # 1 simulated second takes 1 real second
  random_seed: 42  # the same arrival times on every run

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 1}

services:
  # Every order takes exactly 1.5 seconds to pack
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5}

arrivals:
  # One order every 2 seconds on average; each arrival spawns pack_order
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    # The value of the finished event
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

egress:
  - type: Console

run:
  until: 20
docs/snippets/tutorials/first_shop.py
"""The First Simulation tutorial: the shop, with the SimulationContext builder.

One packer, orders arriving about every 2 seconds, and 1.5 seconds of packing per
order. Every record is printed to the terminal.
"""

import logging

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

app = (
    # 1 simulated second = 1 real second; a seed gives the same arrivals every run
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0, random_seed=42)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
    # Every order takes exactly 1.5 seconds to pack
    .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
    # One order every 2 seconds on average
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
)


@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    # Requests a packer, waits the packing time, releases the packer.
    # The returned dictionary is the value of the finished event.
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        # Waits for the next arrival and returns the new order, keyed orders-1, ...
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
        task_id += 1


app.add_egress(ConsoleEgress())

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(until=20)
docs/snippets/tutorials/first_shop_low_level.py
"""The First Simulation tutorial: the shop, on the low-level API.

One packer, orders arriving about every 2 seconds, and 1.5 seconds of packing per
order. Every record is printed to the terminal.
"""

import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=1)},
)
SEED = 42  # the same arrival times on every run


def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id):
    """One order: wait for a packer, pack it, release the packer."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        service = env.registry.get_config(path_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(service))
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers):
    """Starts one pack_order for every arrival, keyed orders-1, orders-2, ..."""
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id))
        task_id += 1


SINKS = [ConsoleEgress()]  # passed to env.setup_egress in run below


def run(until=20, factor=1.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress(SINKS)

    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    sampler = Sampler(seed=SEED)

    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, packers))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

Next, Queues and Capacity asks how many packers keep the wait short.

docs.title: A Flow of Tasks
docs.text: Until now an order was one task: it was packed and left. A real order is picked from the shelves, packed and shipped; sometimes an item is out of stock, and sometimes a parcel fails its check and is packed again. This page asks: how do orders move through pick, pack and ship? It answers with two shares: how many orders go to backorder, and how many parcels are packed again.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text:
Three tasks in a row, pick_order, pack_order and ship_order; a backorder delay for an order picked while the shelf of boxes from Stock is empty; and an express attribute that each order carries. The shop has two pickers and two packers, orders at 0.4 a second and express orders at 0.1, and a delivery of 53 boxes every 100 seconds, a little more than orders take. It runs for an hour.

Look at the flow first:

docs.title: Chain the Tasks
docs.text:
Choosing where an entity goes next is called routing. In desflow a task, which Tasks and Processes describes, names what follows it with next. next is a task name, which always leads there; a list of when rules, each a condition and a task, where the first rule that holds wins and default catches the rest; or weights, below. A task with no next ends the order's flow.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/flow_of_tasks.yaml:chain
pick_order:
  service: picking
  resource: pickers
  payload: {event_type: order_picked}
  # The first rule that holds wins; default catches the rest
  next:
    when:
      - {condition: "level.stock == 0", task: backorder}
    default: pack_order
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks.py:chain
# The first rule that holds wins; default catches the rest
@app.task(
    service_id="picking",
    resource_id="pickers",
    next={
        "when": [{"condition": "level.stock == 0", "task": "backorder"}],
        "default": "pack_order",
    },
)
def pick_order(task_id: int, context: SimulationContext):
    return {"event_type": "order_picked"}
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks_low_level.py:chain
# The first rule that holds wins; default catches the rest
"pick_order": Router(
    {
        "when": [{"condition": "level.stock == 0", "task": "backorder"}],
        "default": "pack_order",
    }
),

A Router takes the same rules as next and returns the name of the task to start. When a task finishes, its process asks the router and starts the next task as a new process, with the same entity:

docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks_low_level.py:next
entity.attributes.update(SETS.get(name, {}))
upstream = Upstream(task_id, entity.key, entity.attributes, finished)
following = ROUTES[name].choose(upstream, env, levels={"stock": shop["stock"]})
if following is None:
    env.stats.flow_finished(entity.arrival)  # the order leaves the shop
    return
instance = next(counters[following])
env.process(task(env, sampler, shop, following, entity, instance, counters))

In SimPy terms, a process that starts another process with env.process(...) is how one step leads to the next. SimPy and desflow describes processes.

The rule reads level.stock, the level of the container stock, at the moment picking finishes; Stores and Containers describes containers. Each name in a condition says where its value comes from: level. for a store or container, attr. for the entity's attributes, payload. for the finished task's payload, and registry["..."] for a live parameter. Task Flow lists everything a condition can use.

Every event of every task carries the order's key, orders-1, so one order can be followed through its whole flow; task names the task, and instance numbers its runs. Each task has one counter, shared by its arrivals and by next, so a re-pick after a backorder gets a new id. In the full builder file the arrival loops take the id from context.next_instance("pick_order"); the low-level file keeps one counters entry per task.

docs.title: Out of Stock
docs.text:
An order picked while the shelf is empty waits for the supplier for a minute, then is picked again. The wait uses no picker or packer, so backorder has a service and no resource: a timed step. It publishes started at once, with no queued event, waits the sampled time, and publishes its finished event:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/flow_of_tasks.yaml:backorder
backorder:
  # A timed step: a service and no resource, so it starts at once
  service: supplying
  payload: {event_type: order_backordered}
  # Applied to the order's attributes when the step finishes
  set: {backordered: 1}
  next: pick_order
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks.py:backorder
# A timed step: a service and no resource, so it starts at once. `set` is applied
# to the order's attributes when the step finishes.
@app.task(service_id="supplying", set={"backordered": 1}, next="pick_order")
def backorder(task_id: int, context: SimulationContext):
    return {"event_type": "order_backordered"}
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks_low_level.py:backorder
"backorder": Router("pick_order"),
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks_low_level.py:set
# Applied to the order's attributes when the step finishes
SETS = {"backorder": {"backordered": 1}}

next: pick_order sends the order back to an earlier task. A route back is allowed anywhere in a flow.

docs.title: Rework
docs.text:
One parcel in 20 fails its check and is packed again. Sending work back to a task it has passed is called rework. weights chooses the next task at random, in proportion to the weights, from a random stream of the routing task's own, route.pack_order, so a seeded run repeats and the choice does not change any other draw:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/flow_of_tasks.yaml:rework
pack_order:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  get: {container: stock, amount: 1}
  payload: {event_type: order_packed}
  # One parcel in 20 fails its check and is packed again
  next:
    weights: {ship_order: 95, pack_order: 5}
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks.py:rework
# One parcel in 20 fails its check and is packed again
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    get={"container": "stock", "amount": 1},
    next={"weights": {"ship_order": 95, "pack_order": 5}},
)
def pack_order(task_id: int, context: SimulationContext):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks_low_level.py:rework
# One parcel in 20 fails its check and is packed again; the generator is set
# in run below
"pack_order": Router({"weights": {"ship_order": 95, "pack_order": 5}}),

The low-level router needs a generator to draw from: ROUTES["pack_order"].rng = sampler.generator("route.pack_order") in run, the stream the builder uses.

docs.title: Carry Attributes
docs.text:
An order is an entity with attributes: values it carries from task to task, such as whether it is express. The arrival gives each new entity its starting attributes, and set on a task changes them when the task finishes, as backorder does with backordered: 1:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/flow_of_tasks.yaml:attributes
arrivals:
  # Each order starts with the attributes given here, read as attr.<name>
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.4, spawn: pick_order, attributes: {express: 0}}
  express: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.1, spawn: pick_order, attributes: {express: 1}}
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks.py:attributes
# Each order starts with the attributes given here, read as attr.<name>
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.4, attributes={"express": 0})
app.add_arrival("express", dist="exponential", rate=0.1, attributes={"express": 1})
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks_low_level.py:attributes
# Each order starts with the attributes given here, read as attr.<name>
ATTRIBUTES = {"orders": {"express": 0}, "express": {"express": 1}}

Entity(key, arrival, attributes) is the order, created by the arrival process; the full file below shows it.

Attributes are not published. A condition reads them as attr.express, and a payload includes them only when it asks: ship_order names express and backordered, so its finished event carries both. This is orders-172, which was picked while the shelf was empty, backordered, picked again and packed twice:

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
How do orders move through pick, pack and ship? Most go straight through, and a few go to backorder or are packed again. The run publishes the finished count of every task at the end, with stats: basic:

Task Finished in the hour pick_order 1,857 backorder 80 pack_order 1,849 ship_order 1,775

4.3% of picks led to backorder (80 of 1,857), and 4.0% of parcels were packed again (74 of 1,849 packs did not lead to a shipment). The weights ask for 5%; the run drew a few less.

docs.title: Why It Works
docs.text: In a flow, each task's arrival rate follows from the rates into it and the routing weights: this is flow balance. Every pack leads to a shipment with probability 0.95, so each order is packed 1 ÷ 0.95 = 1.05 times on average, and the packers see 5% more work than there are orders. A rework loop raises utilisation in the same way, which is why it belongs in the load you work out before running. Task Flow describes routing in full.

docs.title: Full Files
Measuring a Run
docs.text: Most of the last three pages read one number, the mean wait. A run knows much more: how busy the packers were, how long the queue was, how many orders were packed, and how long the slowest one waited. This page asks: what does a run tell me?

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: stats: typical, the built-in statistics at the level that includes waits. The model simulates the busy hour with 3 packers and the measured packing times that Choosing Inputs chose.

docs.title: Switch On Statistics
docs.text:
desflow keeps statistics about a run as it goes, and publishes them as telemetry every 10 simulation seconds and once more at the end. They are off by default, because most runs only generate data. A level switches them on, and each level answers one more question:

Level Question it answers Adds none nothing (the default) minimal What is happening now? each resource's capacity, in_use, queue_length and utilization basic How much got done, and how busy was it? finished counts, and utilization_avg and queue_length_avg over time typical How long did orders take? each task's wait_mean, wait_max, service_mean and service_max all How long did the slowest take? each task's wait_p50, wait_p95 and wait_p99, and the same for service

Each level includes the ones above it. Switch on typical:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/measuring_a_run.yaml:stats
# Counts, time averages, and the mean and maximum wait and service, every 10 s
stats: typical
docs/snippets/tutorials/measuring_a_run.py:stats
# Counts, time averages, and the mean and maximum wait and service, every 10 s
.with_stats("typical")
docs/snippets/tutorials/measuring_a_run_low_level.py:stats
# Counts, time averages, and the mean and maximum wait and service, every 10 s
env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=10)

The environment keeps the statistics in env.stats. Resources report their own changes, but a low-level process has no task for desflow to watch, so it reports each step itself: env.stats.task_queued, task_started and task_finished with the task's name and instance id, and flow_finished when the order leaves the shop. The full file below shows them.

The statistics are telemetry, so they reach every sink, and they can also be read in Python at the end of the run:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/measuring_a_run.yaml:read
# The statistics are telemetry, so every sink receives them
egress:
  - type: Console
docs/snippets/tutorials/measuring_a_run.py:read
if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(until="1 h")
    # The statistics are telemetry, so the console printed them; read them here too
    for name, value in app.env.stats.readings().items():
        print(f"{name} = {value}")
docs/snippets/tutorials/measuring_a_run_low_level.py:read
if __name__ == "__main__":
    env = run()
    # The statistics are telemetry, so the console printed them; read them here too
    for name, value in env.stats.readings().items():
        print(f"{name} = {value}")

Every name has the same form, <sim_id>.stats.<kind>.<name>.<statistic>, such as Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean. These are the statistics published at the end of the hour:

[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.capacity', 'value': 3}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.in_use', 'value': 3}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.queue_length', 'value': 8}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization', 'value': 100.0}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization_avg', 'value': 86.56336659179189}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.queue_length_avg', 'value': 2.405756864104584}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.finished', 'value': 6250}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean', 'value': 1.3816663590146558}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_max', 'value': 9.378296391499589}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.service_mean', 'value': 1.4953759999999972}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.service_max', 'value': 2.7000000000000455}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.flows.orders.finished', 'value': 6250}

tasks.pack_order.finished counts the orders the task finished, and flows.orders.finished counts the orders that left the shop, named by the arrival that started them; with one task the two are equal. The mean wait is 1.38 seconds, not the 1.35 seconds of the empirical candidate in Choosing Inputs, although both use the same 40 measured packing times. The service is now called packing, so it draws from its own stream, service.packing, and the times come in another order; Randomness and Seeds explains why.

docs.title: Counts and Averages Over Time
docs.text:
The statistics are of two kinds. A count, such as finished, adds one for each order. An average over time, such as utilization_avg or queue_length_avg, weighs each value by how long it lasted. Look at the area under the number of busy packers:

desflow adds the area every time the value changes, so the average is exact at any moment. A reading taken now and then, such as every 10 seconds, sees only the value at that instant. The queue in the first five minutes of the hour shows the difference:

The queue rises and falls many times between two readings, and a handful of readings can land on high points by chance. Here they average 2.60 orders, while the queue held 2.19 orders on average over the same five minutes.

docs.title: Wait and Service
docs.text:
The time each order spends in the shop has two parts, both measured from the task's own events:

  • wait runs from queued to started: the time spent waiting for a packer;
  • service runs from started to the finished event: the time spent being packed.

service_mean is 1.50 seconds, the mean of the measured times, and service_max is 2.7 seconds, the longest of them, so the model draws what it was given. wait_max is 9.38 seconds: one order waited almost seven times as long as the average one.

docs.title: Result
docs.text: What does a run tell me? One hour of the busy shop tells you that the packers were busy 86.6% of the time on average, the queue held 2.41 orders on average, an order waited 1.38 seconds on average and 9.38 seconds at most, and 6,250 orders were packed.

docs.title: Why It Works
docs.text: The numbers check each other. Little's Law says that the average number waiting equals the rate at which orders arrive times the average time each waits. 6,250 orders in 3,600 seconds is 1.74 a second, and 1.74 × 1.38 = 2.40, which is queue_length_avg. The utilisation checks the same way: 1.74 orders a second × 1.50 seconds ÷ 3 packers = 0.87. A set of statistics that fails a check like this one points to a mistake in the model or in how it is read. Statistics describes how each one is computed, and the Statistics reference lists every name each level publishes.

"""The Measuring a Run tutorial: the busy hour, with built-in statistics, builder.

Three packers, orders at 1.8 a second and the measured packing times. Every record,
the statistics included, is printed to the terminal, and the script prints the final
statistics again at the end.
"""

import logging

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

# The 40 packing times measured at the bench, in seconds
MEASURED = [
    1.5, 2.5, 2.4, 1.2, 1.3, 1.2, 1.8, 1.4, 2.0, 0.7,
    2.7, 1.4, 1.9, 1.4, 1.3, 1.8, 2.0, 1.4, 1.4, 1.9,
    1.1, 0.8, 1.7, 1.1, 0.7, 1.1, 1.2, 0.9, 0.8, 1.5,
    2.1, 1.3, 1.1, 1.7, 1.9, 1.3, 1.8, 2.2, 1.4, 1.1,
]  # fmt: skip

app = (
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=3, max_cap=10)
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=1.8)
    .add_service("packing", dist="empirical", values=MEASURED)
    # Counts, time averages, and the mean and maximum wait and service, every 10 s
    .with_stats("typical")
    .add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
)


@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
        task_id += 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(until="1 h")
    # The statistics are telemetry, so the console printed them; read them here too
    for name, value in app.env.stats.readings().items():
        print(f"{name} = {value}")
docs/snippets/tutorials/measuring_a_run_low_level.py
"""The Measuring a Run tutorial: the busy hour, with built-in statistics, low-level.

Three packers, orders at 1.8 a second and the measured packing times. The order
process reports each step to the environment's statistics, which publish them as
telemetry; the script prints the final statistics again at the end.
"""

import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

# The 40 packing times measured at the bench, in seconds
MEASURED = [
    1.5, 2.5, 2.4, 1.2, 1.3, 1.2, 1.8, 1.4, 2.0, 0.7,
    2.7, 1.4, 1.9, 1.4, 1.3, 1.8, 2.0, 1.4, 1.4, 1.9,
    1.1, 0.8, 1.7, 1.1, 0.7, 1.1, 1.2, 0.9, 0.8, 1.5,
    2.1, 1.3, 1.1, 1.7, 1.9, 1.3, 1.8, 2.2, 1.4, 1.1,
]  # fmt: skip

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=1.8)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="empirical", values=MEASURED)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=3, max_cap=10)},
)


def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id):
    """One order, which reports each step to the statistics."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})
    env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)
    env.stats.flow_finished("orders")  # the order leaves the shop


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers):
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, f"orders-{task_id + 1}", task_id))
        task_id += 1


def run(until=3600, factor=0.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])
    # Counts, time averages, and the mean and maximum wait and service, every 10 s
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=10)
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    env.process(order_generator(env, Sampler(seed=42), packers))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


if __name__ == "__main__":
    env = run()
    # The statistics are telemetry, so the console printed them; read them here too
    for name, value in env.stats.readings().items():
        print(f"{name} = {value}")

Next, Trusting Results asks whether one run is enough.

docs.title: Priorities
docs.text: A quarter of the shop's orders are now express: the customer paid for speed. With one packer and 0.6 orders a second, every order waits about 5 seconds. This page asks: can express orders jump the queue? And what does that cost the others?

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: An express arrival whose task has priority: 0, while regular orders keep priority: 1, and a packer that serves its queue by priority. The shop is the one from First Simulation, one packer and 1.5 seconds of packing, with regular orders at 0.45 a second and express orders at 0.15, run for an hour.

docs.title: Order the Queue
docs.text:
Which waiting entity a resource serves next is its queue discipline. The usual one is first in, first out (FIFO); others are last in, first out (LIFO), and by priority. Look at four requests that join a queue while the packer is busy, and the order each discipline serves them in:

SimPy has a PriorityResource for the priority discipline, and a PriorityStore for items. In desflow every resource has a queue: fifo (the default), lifo or priority. Under priority the lowest number goes first, and requests with the same priority are served first in, first out:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/priorities.yaml:queue
resources:
  # The packer serves the lowest priority first, the oldest first among equals
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 4, queue: priority}
docs/snippets/tutorials/priorities.py:queue
# The packer serves the lowest priority first, the oldest first among equals
app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4, queue=queue)
docs/snippets/tutorials/priorities_low_level.py:queue
# The packer serves the lowest priority first, the oldest first among equals
packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers", queue=queue)

docs.title: Give Express Orders Priority
docs.text:
Each task gives its requests a priority. Express orders get 0, so they are served before any regular order that is waiting; regular orders get 1:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/priorities.yaml:priority
tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    priority: 1
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
  pack_express:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    priority: 0  # served before any regular order that is waiting
    payload: {event_type: express_packed}

Here each task has a fixed number. A priority can also be an expression read from the entity's attributes, which Task Flow describes, such as priority: attr.priority, so each order gets its own. A priority on a task whose resource does not have queue: priority is refused when the file loads, so to run the shop under fifo, remove queue: priority and both priority lines.

docs/snippets/tutorials/priorities.py:priority
@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", priority=rank(1))
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

# Served before any regular order that is waiting
@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", priority=rank(0))
def pack_express(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "express_packed"}

rank gives each task its priority under priority and none under fifo, because a priority on a resource of another order is refused when the run starts. A task's priority can also be an expression such as priority="attr.tier", or a function of the task id and the entity's attributes, such as priority=lambda task_id, attributes: attributes["tier"], so each order gets its own; the attributes exist before the order joins the queue, while its payload does not.

docs/snippets/tutorials/priorities_low_level.py:priority
# Express orders are served before any regular order that is waiting
TASKS = {"orders": ("pack_order", 1), "express": ("pack_express", 0)}
docs/snippets/tutorials/priorities_low_level.py:request
# Under fifo and lifo the priority is ignored
with packers.request(priority=priority) as request:

In the low-level API each request carries its priority. A resource whose queue is fifo or lifo ignores it, which is how the same code runs under both orders.

Both kinds of order use the same packer, so they share one queue. The built-in statistics, which Statistics describes, keep the mean wait of each task apart: Shop.stats.tasks.pack_express.wait_mean and Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean.

docs.title: Starvation
docs.text: Priority has a price. A regular order is served only when no express order is waiting, so every express order that arrives while it waits pushes it back. As the shop gets busier this grows quickly: with a quarter of orders express, the regular wait is 2.50 seconds at 0.5 orders a second in all, 3.98 at 0.55 and 6.94 at 0.6, while express orders wait less than a second at all three. If express orders alone kept the packer busy, regular orders would never be served at all: they would starve.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
Can express orders jump the queue? Yes, and the regular orders pay for it. The scripts print the mean wait of each kind of order under each queue order:

fifo     pack_express mean wait  5.84 s
fifo     pack_order   mean wait  5.32 s
priority pack_express mean wait  0.84 s
priority pack_order   mean wait  6.94 s

Under priority, express orders wait 0.84 seconds on average instead of 5.84. Regular orders pay for it: 6.94 seconds instead of 5.32.

docs.title: Why It Works
docs.text: Priority does not make the packer faster, so it cannot remove waiting; it only decides who waits. Weighted by how many orders of each kind arrive, the mean wait is 0.75 × 5.32 + 0.25 × 5.84 = 5.45 seconds under fifo and 0.75 × 6.94 + 0.25 × 0.84 = 5.41 seconds under priority: almost the same total, shared out differently. Resources describes how the queue orders requests.

"""The Priorities tutorial: express orders go before regular ones, builder.

One packer, regular orders at 0.45 a second and express orders at 0.15, and 1.5
seconds of packing. Every record is printed to the terminal, and the script prints
the mean wait of each kind of order under each queue order at the end:
python priorities.py 2>/dev/null shows only those lines.
"""

import logging

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)


def shop(queue: str = "priority") -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop with the packer's queue in `queue` order."""

    def rank(value):
        # A priority counts only under the priority order, and the other orders
        # refuse one, so under fifo the tasks have none
        return value if queue == "priority" else None

    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
        # 0.6 orders a second in all, one in four of them express
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.45)
        .add_arrival("express", dist="exponential", rate=0.15)
        .with_stats("typical", interval=3600)  # the mean wait of each task
        .add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
    )
    # The packer serves the lowest priority first, the oldest first among equals
    app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4, queue=queue)

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", priority=rank(1))
    def pack_order(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    # Served before any regular order that is waiting
    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", priority=rank(0))
    def pack_express(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "express_packed"}


    def loop(arrival, task):
        def generator(context: SimulationContext):
            task_id = 0
            while True:
                order = yield context.wait_for_arrival(arrival)
                context.spawn(task(task_id, entity=order))
                task_id += 1

        return generator

    app.arrival_loop("orders")(loop("orders", pack_order))
    app.arrival_loop("express")(loop("express", pack_express))
    return app


def mean_waits(queue: str) -> dict:
    """Runs one hour and returns the mean wait of each task."""
    app = shop(queue)
    app.run(until="1 h")
    readings = app.env.stats.readings()
    return {
        task: readings[f"Shop.stats.tasks.{task}.wait_mean"]
        for task in ("pack_express", "pack_order")
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for queue in ("fifo", "priority"):
        for task, wait in mean_waits(queue).items():
            print(f"{queue:<8} {task:<12} mean wait {wait:5.2f} s")
docs/snippets/tutorials/priorities_low_level.py
"""The Priorities tutorial: express orders go before regular ones, low-level.

One packer, regular orders at 0.45 a second and express orders at 0.15, and 1.5
seconds of packing. Every record is printed to the terminal, and the script prints
the mean wait of each kind of order under each queue order at the end:
python priorities_low_level.py 2>/dev/null shows only those lines.
"""

import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={
        # 0.6 orders a second in all, one in four of them express
        "orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.45),
        "express": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.15),
    },
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=4)},
)
# Express orders are served before any regular order that is waiting
TASKS = {"orders": ("pack_order", 1), "express": ("pack_express", 0)}


def pack(env, sampler, packers, arrival, key, task_id):
    task, priority = TASKS[arrival]
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task=task, instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued(task, task_id)
    # Under fifo and lifo the priority is ignored
    with packers.request(priority=priority) as request:
        yield request
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        env.stats.task_started(task, task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        event = "express_packed" if arrival == "express" else "order_packed"
        publish({"event_type": event})
    env.stats.task_finished(task, task_id)


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers, arrival):
    config = env.registry.get_config(f"Shop.arrival.{arrival}")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(config))
        key = f"{arrival}-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack(env, sampler, packers, arrival, key, task_id))
        task_id += 1


def run(queue="priority", until=3600, factor=0.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=3600)  # the mean wait of each task
    # The packer serves the lowest priority first, the oldest first among equals
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers", queue=queue)
    sampler = Sampler(seed=42)
    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, packers, "orders"))
    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, packers, "express"))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


def mean_waits(queue: str) -> dict:
    """Runs one hour and returns the mean wait of each task."""
    readings = run(queue).stats.readings()
    return {
        task: readings[f"Shop.stats.tasks.{task}.wait_mean"]
        for task in ("pack_express", "pack_order")
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for queue in ("fifo", "priority"):
        for task, wait in mean_waits(queue).items():
            print(f"{queue:<8} {task:<12} mean wait {wait:5.2f} s")

Next, A Flow of Tasks asks how orders move through picking, packing and shipping.

docs.title: Queues and Capacity
docs.text: In its busy hour the shop gets 1.8 orders a second, and packing still takes 1.5 seconds. One packer cannot keep up. This page asks: how many packers keep the mean wait under 10 seconds?

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: More orders, then more packers. The shop is the one from First Simulation, with the arrival rate of the busy hour, a run of one hour, and the number of packers as a setting you change between runs.

docs.title: Work Out the Load
docs.text:
Before running anything, work out how busy the packers would be. Utilisation is the share of time a resource is busy:

utilisation = arrival rate × mean service time ÷ number of units

The load is the top half of that: 1.8 orders a second × 1.5 seconds = 2.7 packers' worth of work arriving every second. One packer would be busy 270% of the time, which is impossible: it falls further behind with every order.

  • With utilisation below 1 a model is stable: the queue rises and falls, but stays bounded.
  • At 1 or above it is not: the queue grows for as long as the run lasts, and every order waits longer than the one before.

So the shop needs at least 3 packers (2.7 ÷ 3 = 0.9). Each resource in a model has its own utilisation, and the one closest to 1 is the bottleneck: it decides how long everything waits.

Here is the busy hour. The arrival rate is 1.8, and until is one hour of simulation time:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/queues_and_capacity.yaml:load

  factor: 0  # unpaced: the hour runs in about a second
  random_seed: 42

arrivals:
  # The busy hour: 1.8 orders a second, more than one packer can pack
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 1.8, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

egress:
  - type: Console

run:
  until: 1 h

A blueprint takes durations wherever it takes a time, such as until: 1 h and value: 1.5 s; a plain number is seconds. factor: 0 runs the hour unpaced, in about a second, because nobody needs to watch it in real time.

docs.title: Run It With More Packers
docs.text:
The number of packers is the resource's current_cap. Each run sets it once:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/queues_and_capacity.yaml:packers
resources:
  # The number of packers comes from the PACKERS variable, 1 when it is not set
  packers:
    current_cap: ${PACKERS:-1}
    max_cap: 10

${PACKERS:-1} reads the environment variable PACKERS, and uses 1 when it is not set.

docs/snippets/tutorials/queues_and_capacity.py:packers
app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=packers, max_cap=10)
docs/snippets/tutorials/queues_and_capacity_low_level.py:packers
resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=packers, max_cap=10)},

A DynamicResource with a current_cap of 3 behaves like a SimPy resource with three units: a request is granted as soon as any unit is free, so three orders are packed at once. Resources describes how it is built and why.

To read the mean wait, switch on the built-in statistics at the typical level, which keeps the mean wait of every task; Measuring a Run explains the levels.

Now run the hour with 1, 2, 3 and 4 packers:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

done

The Builder and Low-level scripts print one line per run. The YAML runs print the same numbers, as the value of their wait_mean lines:

packers 1: mean wait  1127.21 s
packers 2: mean wait   426.31 s
packers 3: mean wait     1.27 s
packers 4: mean wait     0.20 s

docs.title: Waits Near Full Use
docs.text:
With 2 packers, utilisation is 1.35. The queue grows all hour, so the mean wait says only how long the run was: run two hours and it roughly doubles. With 3 packers, utilisation is 0.9 and the wait settles. With 4 it is 0.675, and almost nobody waits.

A stable model can still wait a long time. Waits grow sharply as utilisation approaches 1, and more variable times make it worse. These are measured mean waits in the queue for one packer with a mean service of 1.5 seconds, each over 200,000 simulated seconds:

  • With exponential service times, the mean wait for one unit is utilisation ÷ (1 − utilisation) × mean service time. At 0.75 that is 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 seconds. Going from 0.9 to 0.95 more than doubles it.
  • With constant service times, as in this shop, the wait is half of that, because no unusually long job holds up the queue. Spread in the service time, or in the gaps between arrivals, always lengthens waits; Choosing Inputs measures it.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
How many packers keep the mean wait under 10 seconds? 3 packers, as the mean wait for 1 to 4 packers shows:

With 3 packers the mean wait is 1.27 seconds. With 2 packers it is over 400 seconds and still growing when the hour ends. The answer is the first number of packers that brings utilisation below 1, because the shop's packing time is constant and 0.9 is not yet close enough to 1 for the wait to pass 10 seconds.

docs.title: Why It Works
docs.text: Three packers serving one queue is the M/M/c model of queueing theory when both the gaps and the service times are exponential, and M/D/c when the service time is constant, as here. For both, the wait, measured in service times, depends on utilisation alone once c is fixed, and grows without limit as utilisation reaches 1, which is what the table shows. To bring a resource below 1, change any term of the utilisation: add units (current_cap), work faster (a shorter service time) or take fewer arrivals (a lower rate). Each is a live parameter, so a running model can be relieved, or overloaded on purpose, as Live Parameters shows. Statistics describes how the mean wait is measured.

"""The Queues and Capacity tutorial: the shop's busy hour, with the builder.

Orders arrive at 1.8 a second and each takes 1.5 seconds to pack. The script runs the
hour once for each number of packers, unpaced, and prints the mean wait of each run.
"""

from desflow import SimulationContext

UNTIL = "1 h"  # the busy hour


def shop(packers: int) -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop in its busy hour, with `packers` packers."""
    app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)  # unpaced
    app.add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
    # The busy hour: 1.8 orders a second, more than one packer can pack
    app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=1.8)
    app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=packers, max_cap=10)
    # The mean wait of pack_order, kept by the run and read at the end
    app.with_stats("typical", interval=3600)

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_generator(context):
        task_id = 0
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
            task_id += 1

    return app


def mean_wait(packers: int) -> float:
    """Runs the busy hour with `packers` packers and returns the mean wait."""
    app = shop(packers)
    app.run(until=UNTIL)
    return app.env.stats.readings()["Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean"]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for packers in range(1, 5):
        print(f"packers {packers}: mean wait {mean_wait(packers):8.2f} s")
docs/snippets/tutorials/queues_and_capacity_low_level.py
"""The Queues and Capacity tutorial: the shop's busy hour, on the low-level API.

Orders arrive at 1.8 a second and each takes 1.5 seconds to pack. The script runs the
hour once for each number of packers, unpaced, and prints the mean wait of each run.
"""

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

UNTIL = 3600  # the busy hour, in seconds


def params(packers: int) -> SimParameter:
    """The shop in its busy hour, with `packers` packers."""
    return SimParameter(
        sim_id="Shop",
        service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
        # The busy hour: 1.8 orders a second, more than one packer can pack
        arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=1.8)},
        resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=packers, max_cap=10)},
    )


def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, task_id):
    """One order, which reports each step to the statistics."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
    env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers):
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, task_id))
        task_id += 1


def run(packers: int, until=UNTIL, factor=0.0):
    """Runs the busy hour with `packers` packers, unpaced, and returns the environment."""
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(params(packers))
    # The mean wait of pack_order, kept by the environment and read at the end
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=3600)
    packers_resource = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    sampler = Sampler(seed=42)
    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, packers_resource))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


def mean_wait(packers: int) -> float:
    """Runs the busy hour with `packers` packers and returns the mean wait."""
    env = run(packers)
    return env.stats.readings()["Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean"]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for packers in range(1, 5):
        print(f"packers {packers}: mean wait {mean_wait(packers):8.2f} s")

Next, Randomness and Seeds asks why each run differs, and how to repeat one.

docs.title: Randomness and Seeds
docs.text: Run the busy shop twice: orders arrive at different times and packing durations vary. That is what a stochastic model does, but it makes a result hard to check or to compare. This page asks: why do runs differ, and how can you reproduce one?

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: A seed, then a second arrival. The model simulates the busy hour from Queues and Capacity, using its answer of 3 packers. Packing times now vary: 1.5 seconds on average, give or take 0.5, drawn from a normal distribution. The run is one minute long.

docs.title: Run Twice
docs.text:
A simulation draws its random times from a random number stream: a long sequence of numbers that looks random but is computed from a starting value, the seed. The same seed gives the same sequence, and so the same run. A run without a seed takes a new seed each time, so two runs give two different sets of records.

desflow never runs without a seed. When you give none, it draws one, uses it, and logs it, so any run can be repeated afterwards:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

Leave random_seed out of the simulation section and run the blueprint twice. Each run logs its seed with the command that repeats it:

No random_seed was given, so this run uses 3166812249. Repeat it with: desflow run randomness_and_seeds.yaml --seed 3166812249

Leave random_seed out of SimulationContext and run the script twice. Each run logs its seed with the argument that repeats it:

No random_seed was given, so this run uses 3166812249. Pass random_seed=3166812249 to repeat it.

The low-level API never draws a seed for you: you pass one to Sampler. A Sampler() with no seed draws nothing at random, and every sample is the distribution's mean (for a truncated_normal, its mean or its low, whichever is higher), which suits a test that needs fixed times. To start from a new seed each run, draw one yourself, for example with secrets.randbelow(2**32), and print it.

docs.title: Fix the Seed
docs.text:
Set the seed once, and every run draws the same numbers:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/randomness_and_seeds.yaml:seed
# The same random numbers on every run; leave it out to draw a new seed
random_seed: 42

desflow run randomness_and_seeds.yaml --seed 7 runs with another seed without editing the file; --seed overrides random_seed.

docs/snippets/tutorials/randomness_and_seeds.py:seed
# The same random numbers on every run; leave it out to draw a new seed
SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
docs/snippets/tutorials/randomness_and_seeds_low_level.py:seed
# The same random numbers on every run, passed to Sampler(seed=SEED) in run below
SEED = 42

Repeating a run exactly is called reproducibility. It is what lets you check a result, show it to someone else, and see what a change to the model does on its own. Pick one order and follow it: the twelfth order, orders-12, has these events on every run with the seed 42:

[EVT] {'sim_ts': 5.993, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-12', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 11, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'queued'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 6.695, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-12', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 11, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'started'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 8.443, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-12', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 11, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_packed'}}

It is queued at 5.993, gets a packer at 6.695 and is packed at 8.443: a wait of 0.702 seconds.

docs.title: Add Returns
docs.text:
Now add returned parcels: about one every 5 seconds, recorded as they arrive. They do not use the packers.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/randomness_and_seeds.yaml:returns
arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 1.8, spawn: pack_order}
  # Returned parcels: about one every 5 seconds
  returns: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.2, spawn: receive_return}

tasks:
  # A return is recorded as it arrives; it does not use a packer
  receive_return:
    payload: {event_type: return_received}
docs/snippets/tutorials/randomness_and_seeds.py:returns
# Returned parcels: about one every 5 seconds
app.add_arrival("returns", dist="exponential", rate=0.2)


@app.task()
def receive_return(task_id: int):
    # A return is recorded as it arrives; it does not use a packer
    return {"event_type": "return_received"}


@app.arrival_loop("returns")
def return_generator(context: SimulationContext):
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        parcel = yield context.wait_for_arrival("returns")
        context.spawn(receive_return(task_id, entity=parcel))
        task_id += 1
docs/snippets/tutorials/randomness_and_seeds_low_level.py:returns
# Returned parcels: about one every 5 seconds
PARAMS.arrival["returns"] = DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.2)


def return_generator(env, sampler):
    """Records each return as it arrives; it does not use a packer."""
    # Once registered, the config draws from sampler.generator("arrival.returns")
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.returns")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        key = f"returns-{task_id + 1}"
        value = {"event_type": "return_received"}
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="receive_return", instance=task_id)
        task_id += 1

Sampler(seed=SEED) makes one generator per name, sampler.generator("arrival.returns"), from the seed and the name. When the registry registers a distribution it names it by its path without the sim id, and sampler.sample(config) draws from the generator of that name. Your own code can take a sequence of its own the same way.

A task with no service and no resource, such as receive_return, takes no time: it publishes its payload as soon as the arrival starts it.

Run it with the seed 42. orders-12 has the same three events as before, at the same times. Adding an arrival changed nothing for the orders, because of how desflow hands out random numbers: each distribution draws from a stream of its own, named by its registry path without the sim id. The orders draw from arrival.orders, packing from service.packing, and the new returns from arrival.returns. Look at the two runs side by side:

With one shared stream, the returns would take some of the numbers the orders and packing used to get, and every later time would shift.

docs.title: Result
docs.text: Why do runs differ, and how can you reproduce one? Runs differ because they start their random number streams from different seeds. Repeat a run by supplying the same seed: random_seed: 42 in the blueprint, random_seed=42 on SimulationContext, Sampler(seed=42) in the low-level API, or desflow run --seed 42. With it, the twelfth order waits 0.702 seconds on every run, and still 0.702 seconds after the returns are added.

docs.title: Why It Works
docs.text: One stream per input means that two versions of a model run with the same seed see the same arrivals and the same service times wherever they share them. A difference between their results then comes from the change, not from different random numbers. This is called common random numbers, and it is how two designs are compared fairly. Arrivals and Services describes how each stream is made, and Distributions lists every family with its parameters.

"""The Randomness and Seeds tutorial: the busy shop, seeded, with returns, low-level.

Orders arrive at 1.8 a second and three packers pack each in 1.5 seconds on average,
give or take 0.5. Returned parcels arrive about every 5 seconds and are recorded as
they arrive. Every record is printed to the terminal.
"""

import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=1.8)},
    # Packing varies: 1.5 seconds on average, give or take 0.5
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="normal", mean=1.5, std=0.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=3, max_cap=10)},
)
# The same random numbers on every run, passed to Sampler(seed=SEED) in run below
SEED = 42


def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id):
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers):
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, f"orders-{task_id + 1}", task_id))
        task_id += 1


# Returned parcels: about one every 5 seconds
PARAMS.arrival["returns"] = DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.2)


def return_generator(env, sampler):
    """Records each return as it arrives; it does not use a packer."""
    # Once registered, the config draws from sampler.generator("arrival.returns")
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.returns")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        key = f"returns-{task_id + 1}"
        value = {"event_type": "return_received"}
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="receive_return", instance=task_id)
        task_id += 1


def run(until=60, factor=0.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    sampler = Sampler(seed=SEED)
    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, packers))
    env.process(return_generator(env, sampler))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

Next, Choosing Inputs asks which distribution fits packing times.

docs.title: Stock
docs.text: Every order needs a box, and boxes come from a shelf that a delivery fills every 100 seconds. Orders take about 50 boxes in that time. This page asks: what happens when stock runs out? It compares deliveries of 60 boxes with deliveries of 40.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: A stock container that packing takes one box from, and a deliveries arrival whose task puts boxes back. The shop is the one from First Simulation: one packer, an order every 2 seconds on average, and 1.5 seconds of packing, run for an hour.

docs.title: Hold Stock
docs.text:
So far each order needed only a packer, a resource that it holds and gives back. Stock is a different thing: a quantity that tasks take away and others add, and that is not given back. In SimPy it is a Container: a level between 0 and a capacity, with get(amount) to take and put(amount) to add. A get waits while the level is too low, and a put waits while there is no room.

In desflow it is a container in the containers section. Its current_cap is the capacity, the most it can hold, and level is what it holds when the run starts:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/stock.yaml:container
containers:
  # Boxes on the shelf: room for 200, and 50 when the run starts
  stock: {current_cap: 200, max_cap: 200, level: 50}
docs/snippets/tutorials/stock.py:container
# Boxes on the shelf: room for 200, and 50 when the run starts
app.add_container("stock", current_cap=200, max_cap=200, level=50)
docs/snippets/tutorials/stock_low_level.py:container
# Boxes on the shelf: room for 200, and 50 when the run starts
containers={"stock": ContainerConfig(current_cap=200, max_cap=200, level=50)},

A ContainerConfig holds the level a container starts at. The DynamicContainer built in run reads it, as the full file below shows.

The run builds the container, as it builds the packers. Look at what can wait on it:

docs.title: Take and Restock
docs.text:
Packing an order takes one box. The task gets its packer first and then its box, so an order that finds the shelf empty waits for stock while it holds the packer:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/stock.yaml:take
pack_order:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  # One box per order, taken once the order has a packer; waits while stock is 0
  get: {container: stock, amount: 1}
  payload: {event_type: order_packed}
docs/snippets/tutorials/stock.py:take
# One box per order, taken once the order has a packer; waits while stock is 0
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    get={"container": "stock", "amount": 1},
)
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}
docs/snippets/tutorials/stock_low_level.py:take
with shop["packers"].request() as request:
    yield request
    # One box per order, taken once the order has a packer; waits while stock is 0
    yield shop["stock"].get(1)

A delivery arrives every 100 seconds, and its task puts the boxes on the shelf. It waits while there is no room for all of them. It has no service and no resource, so it takes no time and publishes its payload once the boxes are on the shelf:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/stock.yaml:restock
# A delivery every 100 seconds
deliveries: {dist: constant, value: 100 s, spawn: restock}
docs/snippets/yaml/stock.yaml:delivery
restock:
  # Adds the delivery to the shelf; waits while there is no room for it all
  put:
    container: stock
    amount: ${DELIVERY:-60}
  payload: {event_type: stock_delivered}

${DELIVERY:-60} reads the environment variable DELIVERY, 60 when it is not set, so DELIVERY=40 desflow run stock.yaml runs the smaller deliveries.

docs/snippets/tutorials/stock.py:restock
# A delivery every 100 seconds
app.add_arrival("deliveries", dist="constant", value=100)

# Adds the delivery to the shelf; waits while there is no room for it all
@app.task(put={"container": "stock", "amount": delivery})
def restock(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "stock_delivered"}

@app.arrival_loop("deliveries")
def delivery_generator(context: SimulationContext):
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        delivery = yield context.wait_for_arrival("deliveries")
        context.spawn(restock(task_id, entity=delivery))
        task_id += 1
docs/snippets/tutorials/stock_low_level.py:restock
def restock(env, shop, delivery, key, task_id):
    """Adds the delivery to the shelf; waits while there is no room for it all."""
    yield shop["stock"].put(delivery)
    value = {"event_type": "stock_delivered"}
    env.publish_event(key, value, task="restock", instance=task_id)


def delivery_generator(env, sampler, shop, delivery):
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.deliveries")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        key = f"deliveries-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(restock(env, shop, delivery, key, task_id))
        task_id += 1

docs.title: Watch the Level
docs.text:
The built-in statistics, which Statistics describes, at the minimal level and above publish each container's capacity, level, getters_waiting and putters_waiting. typical adds the mean wait:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/stock.yaml:watch
# The stock's level and waiting tasks every 10 seconds, and the mean wait at the end
stats: typical
docs/snippets/tutorials/stock.py:watch
# The stock's level and waiting tasks every 10 seconds, and the mean wait
.with_stats("typical")
docs/snippets/tutorials/stock_low_level.py:watch
# The stock's level and waiting tasks every 10 seconds, and the mean wait
env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=10)

With deliveries of 40, the shelf runs out before the second delivery. These are the readings around it, with the packer queue:

[TEL] {'sim_ts': 170.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.queue_length', 'value': 0}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 170.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.level', 'value': 1.0}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 170.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.getters_waiting', 'value': 0}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 180.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.queue_length', 'value': 3}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 180.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.level', 'value': 0.0}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 180.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.getters_waiting', 'value': 1}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 190.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.queue_length', 'value': 8}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 190.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.level', 'value': 0.0}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 190.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.getters_waiting', 'value': 1}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 200.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.queue_length', 'value': 12}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 200.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.level', 'value': 40.0}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 200.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.getters_waiting', 'value': 1}

At 180 seconds the shelf is empty, one order waits for a box, and three more wait behind it for the packer. The delivery at 200 seconds puts 40 boxes on the shelf; the waiting order takes its box at that same moment, just after the reading.

The level is also a registry path, Shop.containers.stock.level, so a scenario step or a message from outside can set it during a run, as a stock count would. Stores and Containers describes what such an update does.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
What happens when stock runs out? Orders wait for boxes, and when deliveries cannot keep up, the wait grows all hour. The level over the first 30 minutes, for both delivery sizes:

With deliveries of 60, the mean wait for packing is 1.93 seconds, and stock runs out only once, just before the first delivery. With deliveries of 40, it is 341.89 seconds, and the shelf is empty for about 40 of every 100 seconds. Deliveries of 40 boxes every 100 seconds support packing at most 0.4 orders a second while 0.5 arrive, so the packer queue grows all hour, as with too few packers on Queues and Capacity. The Builder and Low-level scripts print both:

deliveries of 60: mean wait   1.93 s
deliveries of 40: mean wait 341.89 s

docs.title: Why It Works
docs.text: Stock adds a second queue: orders wait at the shelf as well as at the packer. Because packing takes its packer before its box, the shelf's queue is never longer than the number of packers, and the rest of the orders wait in the packer queue behind it, so an empty shelf also stops the packer. Taking the box first would put the long queue at the shelf and keep the packer free, which suits a task whose resource is scarce. Either way, supply below demand means a queue that grows for as long as the run lasts. Stores and Containers describes both kinds of holding.
