env.registry.update("Shop.resources.lath.current_cap", 3)  # no such path: ignored
env.registry.update("Shop.service.packing.rate", 2.0)  # normal has no rate: ignored
env.registry.update("Shop.containers.stock.level", 150)  # stored as 100, the capacity

docs.title: Script an Experiment
docs.text:
A blueprint's scenario lists changes, each with the simulation time it applies at. Here a second packer starts at 30 seconds, orders arrive twice as fast from one minute, and the extra packer leaves at two minutes:

docs/snippets/yaml/scenario.yaml
# The first blueprint with a scripted experiment: a second packer starts at 30 s,
# orders arrive twice as fast from 1 min, and the extra packer leaves at
# 2 min. Every change lands at exactly that simulation time, on every run.
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0
  random_seed: 1

egress:
  - type: Console

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 3}

services:
  packing: {dist: normal, mean: 4 s, std: 1 s}

arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.2, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

# The packers' capacity and queue every 10 seconds, to see each change land
stats: minimal

scenario:
  - {at: 30, path: Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, value: 2}
  - {at: 1 min, path: Shop.arrival.orders.rate, value: 0.4}
  - {at: 2 min, path: Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, value: 1}

run:
  until: 3 min

A scenario is not a connector. It is a SimPy process that waits on the simulation clock, so each step lands at exactly its at, on every run and at any factor, including 0. Every path is checked against the model's registry when the file loads, so a misspelt path stops the load with its line. LocalIngress waits on the wall clock instead, and an unknown path is only logged when it is due. A scenario and an ingress connector can run together, so a scripted baseline can run while an operator steers over Kafka; when both change the same path, the later write wins.

docs.title: Record What a Change Was For
docs.text:
A detector or an agent that watches the data is scored against what really happened. A scenario step with a record publishes a ground-truth record of it: stream_type: "label", with the step's path, the value before (old) and after (new), and the step's record mapping as label. A step can have a record and no path, for something that happened outside the model, and then path, old and new are null.

docs/snippets/yaml/ground_truth.yaml:record
scenario:
  # Changes the rate and publishes a ground-truth record of the change
  - at: 30
    path: Shop.arrival.orders.rate
    value: 1.5
    record: {fault: order_surge, cause: flash sale}
  # A record with no change, such as a fault planted outside the model
  - at: 45
    record: {fault: label_printer_offline}

Labels go only to sinks with when: labels, and those sinks receive nothing else, so the labels never reach the pipeline under test and a scorer reads them apart from the data:

docs/snippets/yaml/ground_truth.yaml:sinks
egress:
  # The data under test: events and telemetry, and no label
  - type: Console
  # The labels only, for a scorer that checks what a detector found
  - type: Jsonl
    config: {default_path: labels/labels.jsonl}
    when: labels

The labels sink writes one line per label:

{"stream_type":"label","sim_ts":30.0,"timestamp":"...","path":"Shop.arrival.orders.rate","old":0.5,"new":1.5,"label":{"fault":"order_surge","cause":"flash sale"}}
{"stream_type":"label","sim_ts":45.0,"timestamp":"...","path":null,"old":null,"new":null,"label":{"fault":"label_printer_offline"}}

In Python, env.publish_label(label, path=..., old=..., new=...) publishes one, and add_egress(sink, when="labels") or setup_egress(..., labels=[...]) makes a labels sink, as the measuring example shows.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Registration. run(), or register_sim_parameter in the low-level API, flattens the SimParameter into the registry: one DynamicValue per path, holding the value and a change signal, and beside them the configuration objects the paths belong to, such as each DistributionConfig.

An update. registry.update(path, value) applies one change. The checks run in order, and an accepted value reaches the parts that read it:

  • A path that does not exist is logged as a warning, and the update is ignored.
  • A value of another type is converted to the type the path holds, so the string "5" sent to an integer path becomes 5; Python's conversion is used, so 2.5 sent to an integer path becomes 2. A value that cannot be converted is logged as an error and ignored.
  • A distribution parameter is checked on a copy of its configuration, by the rules used at build. One out of range is logged as an error, and the old value stays.
  • A current_cap outside 0 to max_cap, or a container level outside 0 to current_cap, is stored clamped to that range, with a warning. A lower max_cap clamps the stored current_cap the same way.
  • A value equal to the current one changes nothing.
  • Otherwise the value is stored, and the attribute of the configuration object is set too, found by splitting the path at its last dot: Shop.service.packing.mean sets mean on the object at Shop.service.packing. That is why the Sampler, which reads that object at every draw, sees the new value.

Change Signal. Each value has a SimPy Store with one slot as its signal. An update puts a token in it if it is empty, and wait_for_change() waits for that token, so several changes before a waiter wakes give one signal, and one waiting process takes it. Resources, stores and containers already wait on their own paths, so wait only on paths nothing else waits on, such as variables:

docs/snippets/pages/registry.py:wait
def watch_speed(env):
    """Logs the conveyor speed every time it changes."""
    speed = env.registry.get("Shop.variables.conveyor_speed")
    while True:
        yield speed.wait_for_change()
        print(f"t={env.now}: conveyor speed is now {speed.value}")


env.process(watch_speed(env))

A container's level changes with every put and get as well; the registry keeps that level so a reader sees it, without signalling the container again.

docs.title: Under Live Changes
docs.text:
What follows a change:

  • Distributions. The next draw uses the new value. The arrival already being waited for keeps its gap, and a task that has drawn its service time keeps it.
  • Resources, stores and containers. The capacity follows at once, and a container's level follows its path, as Resources and Stores and Containers describe.
  • Variables. The new value is stored; a process reads it with env.registry.get(path).value.

A change is easiest to see in the telemetry. With stats: minimal, the scenario above shows the second packer land:

[TEL] {'sim_ts': 20.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.capacity', 'value': 1}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 30.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.capacity', 'value': 1}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 40.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.capacity', 'value': 2}

The reading at 30 seconds still shows 1: the resource applies a change within the same simulation instant, but after the step that made it, and the reading was taken first. The builder publishes the same readings with with_stats:

docs/snippets/pages/live_parameters.py:telemetry
# The packers' capacity, in use, queue and utilization every 2 seconds
app.with_stats("minimal", interval=2.0)

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• An unknown path is a warning, not an error, for an ingress message or a process; only a scenario is checked when it loads.
  • A family is fixed. There is no path that turns a normal into an exponential; that is a new model.
  • Several changes, one signal. A process waiting on a path wakes once for several changes made before it runs, and reads the latest value.
  • Ingress lands on the wall clock. A message's change lands at whatever simulation time the run has reached when it arrives; a change that must happen at an exact simulation time is a scenario step.

docs.title: Low-level API
docs.text:
This page writes a simulation with SimPy and the environment directly: a packing team with a stock of boxes and a store of packed orders, every step written by hand. It builds on SimPy and desflow, which describes the SimPy constructs, and on Builder API, which writes the same kind of model for you.

Use the low-level API when you need what the builder does not do: several resources held at once, as in Multi-Resource Handoffs; resources created while the run goes on, as in Dynamic Topology; or events of your own shape. A builder or blueprint model can also start a low-level process with add_process, as Tasks and Processes shows.

A low-level script takes these steps, in this order:

docs.title: Create the Environment
docs.text:
docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:imports
import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    ContainerConfig,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicContainer,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    DynamicStore,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
    time_to_seconds,
)
docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:environment
env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)  # unpaced; 1.0 follows the wall clock

factor sets the pacing: 1.0 follows the wall clock, and 0.0 runs as fast as possible. logical_start_time and go_live_at work as Time and Pacing describes.

docs.title: Register the Parameters
docs.text:
docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:parameters
env.registry.register_sim_parameter(
    SimParameter(
        sim_id="Shop",
        arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
        service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="normal", mean=1.5, std=0.3)},
        resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=3)},
        containers={"boxes": ContainerConfig(current_cap=100, max_cap=100, level=100)},
        stores={"finished": CapacityConfig(current_cap=50, max_cap=50)},
        variables={"boxes_per_order": 1.0},
    )
)

One SimParameter holds every parameter of one simulation under its sim_id. Registering it gives each value a path, such as Shop.arrival.orders.rate, and only the registered paths exist. Live Parameters lists the paths.

docs.title: Attach the Connectors
docs.text:
docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:connectors
env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])  # starts the egress thread
# env.setup_ingress([KafkaIngress(...)]) would start the ingress thread
env.setup_stats("Shop", "basic", interval=60)  # readings and counts every minute

setup_egress starts the egress thread, which writes every record the processes publish. setup_ingress starts the ingress thread for parameter changes from outside, and setup_stats switches on the built-in statistics. Egress lists the arguments of setup_egress, including a warm-up and labels sinks.

docs.title: Create Resources, Containers and Stores
docs.text:
docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:resources
packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")  # reads Shop.resources.packers.*
boxes = DynamicContainer(env, "Shop", "boxes")  # starts at its level, 100
finished = DynamicStore(env, "Shop", "finished")
sampler = Sampler(seed=42)  # a random stream per distribution, from one seed

Each reads its capacity from the registry when it is created, so the parameters must be registered first, and adds itself to the statistics. Sampler(seed=42) gives each registered distribution a random stream of its own, so a run repeats exactly, as Arrivals and Services describes.

docs.title: Write the Processes
docs.text:
A process is a SimPy generator: it yields to wait, and publishes records as it goes. This one does what @app.task does in the builder, with a box from stock and a store for the result. It publishes each event with the entity key, the task's name and its instance id, and reports each step to the statistics:

docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:order
def order(env, key, task_id):
    """One order: queue for a packer, take a box, pack, then store the result."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)  # what @app.task reports for you
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        count = env.registry.get("Shop.variables.boxes_per_order").value
        yield boxes.get(count)  # waits if the stock is too low
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        yield finished.put({"order": key})
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})
    env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)
    env.stats.flow_finished("orders")

The service time is drawn once the order has a packer and a box, from the configuration the registry holds at that moment, so a change made while it waited still applies to it.

The arrival loop keeps the configuration object rather than a copy of the rate, so the next draw uses whatever rate the registry holds. It gives each order its key, orders-1, orders-2:

docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:arrivals
def arrivals(env):
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")  # the live config object
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))  # each draw reads the current rate
        env.process(order(env, f"orders-{task_id + 1}", task_id))  # the entity key
        task_id += 1

A reading of your own is a process that publishes at an interval; publish_telemetry uses the name exactly as given:

docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:telemetry
def telemetry(env):
    """A reading of your own, beside the built-in statistics."""
    while True:
        env.publish_telemetry("Shop.boxes_per_packer", boxes.level / packers.capacity)
        yield env.timeout(10.0)

A process can also change the simulation itself, through the registry, as a connector or a scenario would:

docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:control
def refill_and_rush(env):
    """Refills boxes every minute, and doubles arrivals after five minutes."""
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(60.0)
        missing = boxes.capacity - boxes.level
        if missing > 0:  # SimPy refuses a put of 0
            yield boxes.put(missing)
        if env.now >= 300 and env.registry.get("Shop.arrival.orders.rate").value < 1.0:
            env.registry.update("Shop.arrival.orders.rate", 1.0)
            env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 2)

docs.title: Start the Processes and Run
docs.text:
docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:start
env.process(arrivals(env))
env.process(telemetry(env))
env.process(refill_and_rush(env))
docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:run
logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)
try:
    env.run(until=time_to_seconds("10 min"))  # until is in simulation seconds
finally:
    env.teardown()  # flushes the buffers and stops the threads

ConsoleEgress writes each record as a log line at INFO level, so logging is switched on first. env.run is SimPy's, so until is a number of simulation seconds; time_to_seconds converts a duration such as "10 min". teardown in finally publishes the last statistics, flushes the last records and stops both threads, even when the run stops with Ctrl+C or an error.

docs.title: What It Does for You
docs.text: Little: the environment paces the clock, holds the registry, writes records on the egress thread and keeps the statistics that setup_stats switches on. Everything else is your code. Builder API lists what SimulationContext.run() writes for you on top of the same steps.

docs.title: Errors and Limits
docs.text:
Nothing is checked before the run as a whole. Each call checks only what it reads, when it runs:

  • An unregistered path raises KeyError when a resource, a process or a registry.get asks for it, so register the parameters before creating anything that reads them.
  • A record without egress is dropped. Until setup_egress runs, publish_event and publish_telemetry do nothing, without an error.
  • A Sampler() with no seed draws nothing at random. Every sample is the distribution's mean (for a truncated_normal, its mean or its low, whichever is higher), so give it a seed.

The low-level API has no limits of its own: anything SimPy can model, a process can do.

docs.title: Full Script
docs.text:
Full script

The complete file, which the documentation tests run:

docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py
"""A complete low-level simulation, as the Low-level API page explains it step by step.

One packing team with a stock of boxes and a store of packed orders. Run it with
`python low_level.py`: it runs unpaced for 10 simulation minutes and prints every record
to the terminal.
"""

import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    ContainerConfig,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicContainer,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    DynamicStore,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
    time_to_seconds,
)

env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)  # unpaced; 1.0 follows the wall clock

env.registry.register_sim_parameter(
    SimParameter(
        sim_id="Shop",
        arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
        service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="normal", mean=1.5, std=0.3)},
        resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=3)},
        containers={"boxes": ContainerConfig(current_cap=100, max_cap=100, level=100)},
        stores={"finished": CapacityConfig(current_cap=50, max_cap=50)},
        variables={"boxes_per_order": 1.0},
    )
)

env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])  # starts the egress thread
# env.setup_ingress([KafkaIngress(...)]) would start the ingress thread
env.setup_stats("Shop", "basic", interval=60)  # readings and counts every minute

packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")  # reads Shop.resources.packers.*
boxes = DynamicContainer(env, "Shop", "boxes")  # starts at its level, 100
finished = DynamicStore(env, "Shop", "finished")
sampler = Sampler(seed=42)  # a random stream per distribution, from one seed


def order(env, key, task_id):
    """One order: queue for a packer, take a box, pack, then store the result."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)  # what @app.task reports for you
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        count = env.registry.get("Shop.variables.boxes_per_order").value
        yield boxes.get(count)  # waits if the stock is too low
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        yield finished.put({"order": key})
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})
    env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)
    env.stats.flow_finished("orders")


def arrivals(env):
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")  # the live config object
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))  # each draw reads the current rate
        env.process(order(env, f"orders-{task_id + 1}", task_id))  # the entity key
        task_id += 1


def telemetry(env):
    """A reading of your own, beside the built-in statistics."""
    while True:
        env.publish_telemetry("Shop.boxes_per_packer", boxes.level / packers.capacity)
        yield env.timeout(10.0)


def refill_and_rush(env):
    """Refills boxes every minute, and doubles arrivals after five minutes."""
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(60.0)
        missing = boxes.capacity - boxes.level
        if missing > 0:  # SimPy refuses a put of 0
            yield boxes.put(missing)
        if env.now >= 300 and env.registry.get("Shop.arrival.orders.rate").value < 1.0:
            env.registry.update("Shop.arrival.orders.rate", 1.0)
            env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 2)


env.process(arrivals(env))
env.process(telemetry(env))
env.process(refill_and_rush(env))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
    )
    try:
        env.run(until=time_to_seconds("10 min"))  # until is in simulation seconds
    finally:
        env.teardown()  # flushes the buffers and stops the threads
    assert (
        packers.capacity == 2
        and env.registry.get("Shop.arrival.orders.rate").value == 1.0
    )
    assert len(finished.items) > 0

docs.title: Resources: DynamicResource
docs.text: A resource is what an entity must hold while it works, and may have to wait for. This page shows how to declare one, how its queue is ordered, how it hands out units, and what happens when its capacity changes during a run.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: A resource is a number of identical units: packers, packing benches, checkout lanes, loading bays. A task asks for one unit, waits in the resource's queue while every unit is busy, holds the unit while it works, and gives it back. How many units there are is the resource's capacity, and it can change while the run goes on, as when packers go on a break.

docs.title: Declare a Resource
docs.text:
A resource has a current_cap, the number of units now, and a max_cap, the most a live change can set. run() builds a DynamicResource for each one the context declares; in the low-level API you build it after registering the parameters:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/resources.yaml:queue-order
resources:
  # fifo (the default), lifo or priority; priority serves the lowest number first,
  # and equal priorities first in, first out
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 4, queue: priority}
docs/snippets/pages/resources.py:declare
app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0)
# fifo (the default), lifo or priority
app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4, queue="priority")
docs/snippets/pages/resources.py:resource
packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")  # capacity from the registry: 2


def order(env, order_id):
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request  # waits until a unit is free
        yield env.timeout(10.0)  # holds the unit for 10 s
    # leaving the with block releases the unit

packers.request() is an event that happens when a unit is granted, and leaving the with block gives the unit back. A request whose with block is left before it is granted, for example after a timeout, is cancelled and never takes a unit.

docs.title: Queue Order
docs.text:
queue sets the order in which a resource serves the requests waiting for it:

  • fifo, the default: the oldest first;
  • lifo: the newest first;
  • priority: the lowest priority number first, and the oldest first among equal priorities.

Four requests that join while the only unit is busy are served in these orders:

docs/snippets/pages/resources.py:queue-order
def served_order(queue):
    """Four requests join while the only bench is busy; returns who is served when."""
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(
        SimParameter(
            sim_id="Shop",
            resources={"benches": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=1)},
        )
    )
    bench = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "benches", queue=queue)
    served = []

    def use(name, priority, after=0.0):
        yield env.timeout(after)
        # The priority counts only under the priority order
        with bench.request(priority=priority) as request:
            yield request
            served.append(name)
            yield env.timeout(1.0)

    env.process(use("first", 1))  # takes the bench at once
    for name, priority in [
        ("orders-1", 1),
        ("express-1", 0),
        ("orders-2", 1),
        ("express-2", 0),
    ]:
        env.process(use(name, priority, after=0.1))  # all join while it is busy
    env.run(until=10)
    return served[1:]


for queue in ("fifo", "lifo", "priority"):
    print(f"{queue:<8} {', '.join(served_order(queue))}")

fifo     orders-1, express-1, orders-2, express-2
lifo     express-2, orders-2, express-1, orders-1
priority express-1, express-2, orders-1, orders-2
capacity 2, in use 4

The last line is the capacity drop that Under Live Changes describes, below. The same four requests, drawn:

docs.title: Task Priority
docs.text:
Under queue: priority, each task gives its requests a priority: a number, the same for every run of the task; an expression, read when the task joins the queue, such as attr.tier for the entity's attribute tier; or, in the builder, a function of the task id and the entity's attributes. The attributes exist before the request queues, and the task's own payload does not, so a priority cannot read it; an expression can read the previous task's payload as payload.<field>.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/resources.yaml:priority
tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    # A number, or an expression read when the order joins the queue
    priority: attr.tier
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
docs/snippets/pages/resources.py:priority
app = (
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0, random_seed=42)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4, queue="priority")
    .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5, attributes={"tier": 2})
)


# Each order's own priority, from its attributes, when it joins the queue;
# a number or an expression such as "attr.tier" works too
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    priority=lambda task_id, attributes: attributes["tier"],
)
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

A low-level process passes the priority to the request: packers.request(priority=entity.attributes["tier"]), as the queue-order example above does. A resource whose queue is fifo or lifo ignores it.

A priority on a task whose resource does not have queue: priority is refused: when the blueprint loads, or when run() starts. Priorities shows what priority does to waits.

docs.title: Registry Paths and Readings
docs.text: Each resource has two registry paths, <sim_id>.resources.<name>.current_cap and .max_cap, which a scenario, an ingress message or a process can change; Live Parameters explains how. With statistics at the minimal level or above, each resource publishes four readings, such as Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization: capacity, in_use, queue_length and utilization, the busy units as a percentage of the capacity. Statistics lists what the other levels add.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
A DynamicResource is built from SimPy parts. Each request waits in a SimPy PriorityStore, ranked by the queue order and a sequence number, so requests that rank the same are served in the order they arrived. Free units are tokens in a SimPy Container, the pool, whose size follows the registry. A dispatcher process waits for a request and a token, and gives the token to the first request:

If the request it takes was cancelled, the dispatcher puts the token back and takes the next. in_use counts the units held by tasks: it goes up when a request is granted and down when a unit is released.

SimPy and desflow. SimPy's Resource serves requests in the order they arrive, and PriorityResource by priority. Both take their capacity when they are created and keep it: capacity has no setter, so assigning a new one raises AttributeError (SimPy 4.1). desflow builds its own resource so the capacity can follow the registry and the queue order can be chosen; the request() call and the with block are SimPy's, so code written for SimPy works unchanged. SimPy and desflow compares the two.

docs.title: Under Live Changes
docs.text:
A change to current_cap takes effect at once, without stopping any work:

  • Growing adds tokens to the pool, and waiting requests start.
  • Shrinking removes idle tokens at once. The units still busy above the new capacity are owed: while tokens are owed, each released token is discarded instead of returning to the pool, so no waiting task starts until the busy units are within the new capacity.
  • Growing again before the owed tokens arrive first cancels them, then adds any difference to the pool.
  • A current_cap outside 0 to max_cap is clamped to that range, with a warning.
  • Lowering max_cap lowers the pool's limit. A current_cap above the new max_cap is stored as max_cap, with a warning.

The example above takes three of five packers off the floor while four orders are being packed: the capacity is 2 at once, and in_use stays 4 until two orders finish. The animation steps through it:

docs/snippets/pages/resources.py:shrink
def breakdown(env):
    """Takes 3 of 5 packers off the floor at t=5 s. Orders being packed are not stopped."""
    env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 5)
    yield env.timeout(5.0)
    env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 2)
    yield env.timeout(0.1)  # the resource applies the change in its own process
    print(f"capacity {packers.capacity}, in use {packers.in_use}")

Until the owed units finish, in_use is above capacity, and the utilization reading is above 100.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• Utilisation decides waits. A resource whose load is at or above its capacity has a queue that grows for as long as the run lasts; Queues and Capacity shows how to work it out.
  • Priority needs queue: priority. A task priority on a resource of another order is a load error, while a low-level request's priority is ignored under fifo and lifo.
  • Priority can starve. Under priority, a request with a high number is served only when no lower number is waiting; if the low numbers alone keep the resource busy, it is never served.
  • One resource per task. A task that needs two resources at once is a process: Multi-Resource Handoffs.
  • A shrink never stops work. A resource that must stop work in progress, such as a breakdown, needs a process: Preemptive Breakdowns.

Amounts and items that tasks take and add, rather than hold, are Stores and Containers.

docs.title: Built-in Statistics
docs.text: A run can measure itself: how busy each resource was, how long tasks waited, how many entities finished. This page shows how to switch the statistics on, what each level publishes and costs, how each value is computed, and how to add readings of your own.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: The built-in statistics are measures that desflow keeps while the run goes on and publishes as telemetry, under fixed names such as Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean. They need no code of yours in the builder or YAML, and they reach every sink like any other telemetry. They are off by default, because most runs only generate data. Measuring a Run reads them on the shop.

docs.title: Choose a Level
docs.text:
A level switches them on. Each level publishes what the levels before it publish, and answers one more question:

Level Question Adds none nothing; the default minimal What is happening now? resources: capacity, in_use, queue_length, utilization; stores and containers: capacity, level, getters_waiting, putters_waiting basic How much got done, and how busy was it? tasks and flows: finished; resources: utilization_avg, queue_length_avg; stores and containers: level_avg typical How long did tasks take? tasks: wait_mean, wait_max, service_mean, service_max all How long did the slowest take? tasks: wait_p50, wait_p95, wait_p99, service_p50, service_p95, service_p99

They are published every interval of simulation time, 10 seconds when it is not given, starting one interval after the start, and once more at the end of the run:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/statistics.yaml:levels
# none (the default), minimal, basic, typical or all, each adding to the one before;
# published every interval of simulation time and once at the end
stats: {level: typical, interval: 1 min}

stats: typical is the short form, with the 10-second interval. The interval takes seconds or a duration.

docs/snippets/pages/built_in_statistics.py:builder-levels
# none (the default), minimal, basic, typical or all, each adding to the one before;
# published every interval of simulation seconds and once at the end
app.with_stats("typical", interval=60)
docs/snippets/pages/built_in_statistics.py:low-level-levels
env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=60)  # before or after the resources

Resources, stores and containers add themselves to env.stats when they are built. Tasks are your own processes, so each reports its steps:

docs/snippets/pages/built_in_statistics.py:low-level-report
# A low-level task reports its own steps to the statistics
env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
with packers.request() as request:
    yield request
    env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
    yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)
env.stats.flow_finished("orders")  # the order leaves the shop

docs.title: Read the Names
docs.text:
Every statistic is published as telemetry named <sim_id>.stats.<kind>.<name>.<statistic>, where the kind is resources, stores, containers, tasks or flows. A flow is named by the arrival that started its entities: Shop.stats.flows.orders.finished counts the orders that left the model. Reference, Statistics lists every name with what it measures. These are the statistics the blueprint above publishes at the end of its two minutes:

[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.capacity', 'value': 2}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.in_use', 'value': 2}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.queue_length', 'value': 6}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization', 'value': 100.0}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization_avg', 'value': 90.79208653095155}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.queue_length_avg', 'value': 1.9083531344309013}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.finished', 'value': 70}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean', 'value': 2.7959715976263215}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_max', 'value': 11.22214686679115}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.service_mean', 'value': 3.0335617388528364}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.service_max', 'value': 6.357944038555676}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.flows.orders.finished', 'value': 70}

In Python the same values are in env.stats.readings(), by name, during or after the run:

docs/snippets/pages/built_in_statistics.py:low-level-read
# Every statistic the level publishes, by its published name
readings = env.stats.readings()
print(f"mean wait {readings['Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean']:.2f} s")

app.env.stats.readings() gives the same from a builder or YAML run.

docs.title: Add Readings of Your Own
docs.text:
Anything else is a custom reading: a function called at an interval of simulation time, which publishes with context.publish(name, value) as <sim_id>.<name>. It can read resources, stores, containers or any registry value.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/statistics.yaml:custom
telemetry:
  # Readings of your own: called as packers_report(context) every 30 seconds
  - interval: 30
    function: !python shop_logic.packers_report

The function is in shop_logic.py, beside the blueprint:

docs/snippets/yaml/shop_logic.py:packers-report
def packers_report(context):
    """A custom reading: orders waiting per packer, and the live arrival rate."""
    packers = context.get_resource("packers")
    waiting = len(packers.queue.items)
    context.publish("waiting_per_packer", waiting / max(packers.capacity, 1))
    rate = context.env.registry.get(f"{context.sim_id}.arrival.orders.rate").value
    context.publish("arrival_rate", rate)  # as Shop.arrival_rate
docs/snippets/pages/built_in_statistics.py:builder-custom
@app.telemetry_loop(interval=30.0)
def packers_report(context: SimulationContext):
    """Readings of your own: orders waiting per packer, and the live arrival rate."""
    packers = context.get_resource("packers")
    waiting = len(packers.queue.items)
    context.publish("waiting_per_packer", waiting / max(packers.capacity, 1))
    rate = context.env.registry.get("Shop.arrival.orders.rate").value
    context.publish("arrival_rate", rate)  # as Shop.arrival_rate

A process that loops, publishes with env.publish_telemetry(name, value) and waits with env.timeout(interval) does the same.

docs.title: Example: Measuring a Run
docs.text:
The measuring example publishes every statistic of the packers and the pack task every 5 minutes, leaves out a 3-minute warm-up, and sends a ground-truth record when packing slows down, to a sink of its own. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

Quick Start

desflow examples get downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

uvpip 
# 1. Install
uv tool install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get measuring --api yaml
cd measuring/yaml

# 3. Run it
desflow run measuring.yaml

# 1. Install
pip install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get measuring --api yaml
cd measuring/yaml

# 3. Run it
desflow run measuring.yaml
examples/yaml/measuring.yaml:measure
# Every level: readings, counts and time averages, mean and maximum wait and service,
# and their 50th, 95th and 99th percentiles, such as Shop.stats.tasks.pack.wait_p95.
stats: {level: all, interval: 5 min}

scenario:
  # Packing slows from 4 to 4.8 seconds on average. The record is the ground truth.
  - at: 12 min
    path: Shop.service.packing.scale
    value: 1.2
    record: {fault: slow_packing, cause: new packing material}

The whole file is examples/yaml/measuring.yaml.

Quick Start

desflow examples get downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

uvpip 
# 1. Install
uv tool install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get measuring --api builder
cd measuring/builder

# 3. Run it
uv run --no-project --with desflow measuring_example.py

# 1. Install
pip install desflow

# 2. Download the example

cd measuring/builder

# 3. Run it
python measuring_example.py
examples/builder/measuring_example.py:fault
def slow_packing(context):
    """Packing slows from 4 to 4.8 seconds on average at 12 minutes, with its label."""
    yield context.env.timeout(720)
    path = "Shop.service.packing.scale"
    registry = context.env.registry
    old = registry.get(path).value
    registry.update(path, 1.2)
    context.env.publish_label(
        {"fault": "slow_packing", "cause": "new packing material"},
        path=path,
        old=old,
        new=registry.get(path).value,
    )


app.add_process(slow_packing)

The whole file is examples/builder/measuring_example.py.

Quick Start

desflow examples get downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

uvpip 
# 1. Install
uv tool install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get measuring --api low-level
cd measuring/low-level

# 3. Run it
uv run --no-project --with desflow measuring_example.py

# 1. Install
pip install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get measuring --api low-level
cd measuring/low-level

# 3. Run it
python measuring_example.py
examples/low-level/measuring_example.py:measure
# Every level, published every 5 minutes, such as Shop.stats.tasks.pack.wait_p95
env.setup_stats("Shop", "all", interval=300)
# The second sink receives the ground-truth records, and nothing else
env.setup_egress(
    [ConsoleEgress(), ConsoleEgress()], labels=[False, True], warmup=WARMUP
)

The whole file is examples/low-level/measuring_example.py.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
The environment keeps one Statistics object, env.stats, which collects nothing until a level above none is set. Its timer publishes every value at each interval, and the teardown publishes them once more.

Readings now. capacity, in_use, queue_length and level are read from the object at the moment of publishing. in_use counts the units held by tasks, so after a capacity drop it can be above capacity, and utilization, in_use ÷ capacity × 100, above 100.

Averages over time. utilization_avg, queue_length_avg and level_avg weigh each value by how long it lasted. Each resource, store and container reports every change, and the statistics add the area under the value since the last change, so the average is exact at any moment rather than sampled:

Counts. finished adds one when a task instance finishes, and a flow's finished adds one when an entity's last task has no next task.

Wait and service. The wait of a task instance runs from its queued step to its started step, and its service from started to finished; a task that never queues, such as a timed step, waits 0. typical keeps a count, a total and a maximum of each, so their cost does not grow with the run. all keeps every observation and computes the percentiles exactly with NumPy's percentile at each publication, so its memory grows with the number of tasks.

Warm-up. A run's warmup resets every statistic once, at that time: the averages start again from zero area, and the counts and observations from zero. An instance that was queued before the reset and starts after it counts with its whole wait. Time and Pacing describes the warm-up.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• Cost. minimal reads a few values at each publication. basic adds a little work at every change of a resource, store or container. typical adds a little at every task step. all keeps every wait and service time in memory for the whole run; use it for runs of thousands of tasks, not for a generator that runs for days.
  • One way to get resource readings. Before 0.21.0, a telemetry entry could publish <resource>.<reading> by name. That shortcut is gone: stats: minimal publishes the same readings, under Shop.stats.resources.<name>.<reading>. telemetry now takes only a function, for readings of your own.
  • One run is one sample. The statistics describe one run with one seed. Values from the same run are not independent of each other, and another seed gives other values; Trusting Results shows what that means for a result.
  • A task appears once it has run. A task's statistics are published from the first time it starts, at typical and all, or finishes, at basic.

docs.title: Stores and Containers: DynamicStore and DynamicContainer
docs.text: A resource is held and given back. Stores and containers hold things that tasks take away and add: items, or an amount. This page shows how to declare them, how tasks put and get, and what a live change does.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
• A store holds items, each one a value of its own: parcels on a shelf waiting for a courier, orders in a buffer. A task puts an item in, and another takes the oldest out.
  • A container holds an amount: boxes in a bin, fuel in a tank, a stock level. A task takes some, and another adds some.

Both have a capacity. A task that takes waits while there is not enough, and a task that adds waits while there is no room. Stock uses a container in the shop.

docs.title: Declare Them
docs.text:
A container has a current_cap, its capacity, the largest amount it holds; a max_cap, the largest capacity a live change can set; and a level, the amount it holds when the run starts, 0 when left out. A store has a current_cap and a max_cap, in whole items, and starts empty. run() builds a DynamicContainer and a DynamicStore for each one the context declares; a store and a container cannot share a name.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/stores_containers.yaml:container
containers:
  # An amount: room for 100 boxes, 20 when the run starts
  stock: {current_cap: 100, max_cap: 100, level: 20}
docs/snippets/yaml/stores_containers.yaml:store
stores:
  # Items: room for 5 parcels, empty when the run starts
  parcels: {current_cap: 5, max_cap: 10}
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:builder-container
# An amount: room for 100 boxes, 20 when the run starts
app.add_container("stock", current_cap=100, max_cap=100, level=20)
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:builder-store
# Items: room for 5 parcels, empty when the run starts
app.add_store("parcels", current_cap=5, max_cap=10)
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:low-level-container
env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)
env.registry.register_sim_parameter(
    SimParameter(
        sim_id="Shop",
        # An amount: room for 100 boxes, 20 when the run starts
        containers={"stock": ContainerConfig(current_cap=100, max_cap=100, level=20)},
        # Items: room for 5 parcels, empty when the run starts
        stores={"parcels": CapacityConfig(current_cap=5, max_cap=10)},
    )
)
stock = DynamicContainer(env, "Shop", "stock")  # starts at the level above, 20
parcels = DynamicStore(env, "Shop", "parcels")

A DynamicContainer built with no init starts at the level its ContainerConfig gives; init= sets another.

docs.title: Take and Add
docs.text:
A task takes with get and adds with put. For a container, each names the container and an amount: a number; an expression, such as payload.boxes for a field of the previous task's payload; or in the builder, a function of the task id and the previous task's payload. The amount is 1 when left out. For a store, each names the store: a put adds the task's finished payload as the item, and a get takes the oldest item and passes it to the task's function as item.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/stores_containers.yaml:take
pack_order:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  # Takes the boxes the previous task's payload names, once it has a packer
  get: {container: stock, amount: payload.boxes}
docs/snippets/yaml/stores_containers.yaml:put
# Adds its finished payload to the store as an item
put: {store: parcels}
payload: {event_type: order_packed}
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:builder-take
# Takes the boxes the previous task's payload names, once it has a packer.
# The amount is a number, an expression, or a function of the task id and the
# previous task's payload, such as lambda task_id, payload: payload["boxes"].
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    get={"container": "stock", "amount": "payload.boxes"},
    put={"store": "parcels"},  # adds the finished payload as an item
)
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


# Takes the oldest parcel, waiting while the store is empty; `item` is that parcel
@app.task(service_id="collecting", get={"store": "parcels"})
def collect(task_id: int, item):
    return {"event_type": "parcel_collected", "parcel": item["event_type"]}
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:low-level-take
def pack(env, order_id):
    yield stock.get(2)  # takes 2 boxes, waiting while fewer are left
    yield parcels.put({"order_id": order_id})  # waits while the store is full


def collect_parcel(env):
    parcel = yield parcels.get()  # waits while the store is empty
    print(f"collected order {parcel['order_id']}; {stock.level:g} boxes left")

get(amount), put(amount), put(item) and get() are SimPy events: yielding one waits until it succeeds, and a store's get() succeeds with the item.

A task with a resource gets its unit first and then takes its get, so it waits for stock while holding the unit. A task adds its put after its service time, then publishes the finished event. Tasks and Processes lists every step.

docs.title: Registry Paths, Readings and Conditions
docs.text:
A container has three registry paths, <sim_id>.containers.<name>.current_cap, .max_cap and .level; a store has <sim_id>.stores.<name>.current_cap and .max_cap. With statistics at the minimal level or above, each publishes four readings, such as Shop.stats.containers.stock.level:

Reading Store Container capacity items it can hold largest amount level items held amount held getters_waiting tasks waiting to get an item tasks waiting to take an amount putters_waiting tasks waiting to put an item tasks waiting to add an amount

basic adds level_avg, the level averaged over time; Statistics describes it. These are the readings of the blueprint above at 30 and 40 seconds, before and after the stock count below:

[TEL] {'sim_ts': 30.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.stores.parcels.level', 'value': 3}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 30.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.stores.parcels.putters_waiting', 'value': 0}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 30.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.level', 'value': 0.0}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 30.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.getters_waiting', 'value': 2}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 40.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.stores.parcels.level', 'value': 5}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 40.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.stores.parcels.putters_waiting', 'value': 2}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 40.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.level', 'value': 38.0}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 40.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.getters_waiting', 'value': 0}

At 30 seconds the bin is empty and two orders wait for boxes; at 40 seconds the count has put 50 boxes in, those two have taken theirs, and the shelf of parcels is full, with two packed orders waiting for room.

A condition in a task's next reads a level as level.<name>, so an order can go to backorder when level.stock == 0, as Task Flow shows.

docs.title: Example: Stock, Parcels and Express Orders
docs.text:
The stock example puts it together: packing takes a box from a container and puts the parcel in a store, a courier collects it, and express orders go first. The stock runs out, so packing waits until a restock at 40 seconds sets the level to 30. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own.

examples/low-level/stock_example.py:pack
def pack(env, sampler, shop, key, priority, task_id):
    """Queued, a packer by priority, a box from stock, packing, then a parcel."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    with shop["packers"].request(priority=priority) as req:
        yield req
        # Waits while the stock is empty
        yield shop["stock"].get(1)
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        payload = {"event_type": "order_packed", "priority": priority}
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        # Waits while the store is full
        yield shop["parcels"].put(payload)
        publish(payload)

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
A container keeps a level between 0 and its capacity, with a queue of getters and a queue of putters. A get succeeds as soon as the level covers its amount, and a put as soon as there is room for all of it; until then each waits in its queue, in the order it arrived:

A store keeps a list of items, up to its capacity. A put adds an item at the end, and a get takes the first, so items leave in the order they came:

SimPy and desflow. Underneath are SimPy's Container and Store, and a PriorityStore for a DynamicStore(..., priority=True) in the low-level API, which hands out the lowest item first. SimPy's capacities are fixed when they are created; desflow's follow the registry, keep the registry's level in step with every put and get, and report each change to the statistics. SimPy and desflow compares the two.

docs.title: Under Live Changes
docs.text:
• Capacity follows current_cap, clamped to between 0 and max_cap. A higher capacity wakes waiting putters. A capacity below what is held destroys nothing: puts wait until enough has been taken.
  • A container's level is set by an update to its level path, as a stock count or a restock from outside would. The new level is clamped to between 0 and current_cap, with a warning, and it wakes both queues: a higher level serves waiting getters, and a lower one can make room for putters.
  • current_cap is the capacity, not a level. A model that used a container's current_cap as a level, such as the wear of a roll, moves it to level.

The stock count in the blueprint above, in each way of writing:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/stores_containers.yaml:level
scenario:
  # A stock count at 30 seconds: the level path sets what the container holds
  - {at: 30, path: Shop.containers.stock.level, value: 50}
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:builder-level
def stock_count(context: SimulationContext):
    """A stock count at 30 seconds: the level path sets what the container holds."""
    yield context.env.timeout(30)
    context.env.registry.update("Shop.containers.stock.level", 50)


app.add_process(stock_count)
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:low-level-level
def stock_count_process(env):
    """A stock count: sets the level; waiting gets and puts are woken."""
    yield env.timeout(30)
    env.registry.update("Shop.containers.stock.level", 50)

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• A container that never refills blocks its getters for good, and a task that waits for stock while holding a resource blocks the resource too. Supply has to keep up with demand, as Stock shows.
  • Whole items. A store's capacity is a whole number, and it holds items, not amounts.
  • No filter. A get takes the oldest item; a get that picks an item by a condition (SimPy's FilterStore) is not available before 1.0.
  • One store or container per get or put. A task has at most one get and one put.

docs.title: Task Flow: the Next Task by Condition or Probability
docs.text: An entity rarely leaves after completing just one task. An order is checked, perhaps wrapped as a gift, packed, sometimes packed again, and shipped. This page shows how a finished task chooses the next one, and what the entity carries from task to task.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
A flow is the sequence of tasks one entity passes through. Each task names what follows it: always the same task, the first of several rules whose condition holds, or a task drawn at random by weight. A rule can send the entity back to a task it has passed, for rework. A task that names nothing ends the flow. The entity keeps its key and its attributes through the whole flow, and every task can read them.

A Flow of Tasks builds a pick, pack and ship flow step by step.

docs.title: Choose the Next Task
docs.text:
next takes one of these forms:

  • A task name, next: pack_order: always that task.
  • Rules, when with an optional default: each rule is a condition and a task. Rules are tried in order. The first matching rule wins, and default applies if none matches. With no default and no matching rule, the flow ends.
  • Weights, below.
  • In the builder, a function that takes the Upstream and returns a task name or None.
YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/task_flow.yaml:condition
check_order:
  payload: {total: 80}
  # Rules are tried in order; the first match wins. Otherwise, use the default.
  next:
    when:
      - {condition: "level.stock == 0", task: backorder}
      - {condition: "payload.total >= 100 or attr.gift == 1", task: wrap_gift}
    default: pack_order
docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:builder-condition
# Rules are tried in order; the first match wins. Otherwise, use the default.
@app.task(
    next={
        "when": [
            {"condition": "level.stock == 0", "task": "backorder"},
            {
                "condition": "payload.total >= 100 or attr.gift == 1",
                "task": "wrap_gift",
            },
        ],
        "default": "pack_order",
    }
)
def check_order(task_id: int):
    return {"total": 80}
docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:low-level-condition
# The same rules as next, as a Router; choose() returns the next task's name
route = Router(
    {
        "when": [{"condition": "attr.gift == 1", "task": "wrap_gift"}],
        "default": "pack_order",
    }
)
order = Entity("orders-1", "orders", {"gift": 0})  # key, arrival, attributes
finished = Upstream(0, order.key, order.attributes, {"total": 80})
assert route.choose(finished, env=None) == "pack_order"

A Router takes the same rules as next. When a task finishes, its process builds the Upstream, asks route.choose(upstream, env, levels=...) for the next task's name, and starts that task with the same entity. env lets a condition read registry[...] and t, and levels, a mapping of store and container names to the objects, lets it read level.<name>.

The condition is evaluated when the task finishes, after its set. payload. reads the payload of the task that just finished, attr. the entity's attributes, level. a store's or container's level, and registry["..."] a live parameter. How It Works lists everything a condition can use.

docs.title: Weights
docs.text:
weights maps task names to numbers, and the next task is drawn in proportion to them. The draw comes from a random stream of the routing task's own, route.<task>, so a seeded run repeats it and it changes no other draw:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/task_flow.yaml:weights
pack_order:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  get: {container: stock, amount: 1}
  payload: {event_type: order_packed}
  # A task drawn in proportion to its weight: one in ten is packed again
  next:
    weights: {ship_order: 9, pack_order: 1}
docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:builder-weights
# A task drawn in proportion to its weight: one in ten is packed again
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    get={"container": "stock", "amount": 1},
    next={"weights": {"ship_order": 9, "pack_order": 1}},
)
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}
docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:low-level-weights
# Weights draw from a generator: the routing task's own stream, as the builder's do
rework = Router({"weights": {"ship_order": 9, "pack_order": 1}})
rework.rng = Sampler(seed=42).generator("route.pack_order")
choices = [rework.choose(finished) for _ in range(1000)]

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
An arrival gives each new entity its starting attributes, and a task's set changes them when the task finishes. Each entity gets its own copy. Attributes are not published: a condition reads them as attr.<name>, and a payload includes them only when it asks.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/task_flow.yaml:attributes
arrivals:
  # Each order starts with these attributes, read as attr.gift
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5, spawn: check_order, attributes: {gift: 0}}
  gifts: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.1, spawn: check_order, attributes: {gift: 1}}
docs/snippets/yaml/task_flow.yaml:set
# Applied to the order's attributes when the task finishes
set: {backordered: 1}

A task's attributes list adds the named attributes to a mapping payload, as ship_order does in the full blueprint.

docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:builder-attributes
# Each order starts with these attributes, read as attr.gift
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5, attributes={"gift": 0})
app.add_arrival("gifts", dist="exponential", rate=0.1, attributes={"gift": 1})
docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:builder-set
# `set` is applied to the order's attributes when the task finishes
@app.task(service_id="supplying", set={"backordered": 1}, next="check_order")
def backorder(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_backordered"}

An Entity(key, arrival, attributes) carries them; the process updates entity.attributes itself after a task, as the low-level tab of A Flow of Tasks shows.

docs.title: Entity Key
docs.text:
Each arrival starts a new entity, keyed by the arrival's name and a counter from 1: orders-1, orders-2. Every event of every task in its flow carries that key as its record key, so a sink can follow one order through the whole flow, and Kafka keeps its events in order on one partition. The builder can replace the key with a function of the counter:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A blueprint uses the default key.

docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:builder-key
# Keys ret-00001, ret-00002 instead of returns-1, from the counter, which starts at 1
app.add_arrival("returns", dist="exponential", rate=0.05, key=lambda n: f"ret-{n:05d}")

The process that creates each Entity gives it its key.

These are the finished events of gifts-5 in the blueprint above: checked while the shelf was empty, backordered, checked again, wrapped, packed and shipped, all under one key:

[EVT] {'sim_ts': 19.216, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'gifts-5', 'task': 'check_order', 'instance': 13, 'value': {'total': 80}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 49.216, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'gifts-5', 'task': 'backorder', 'instance': 1, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_backordered'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 49.216, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'gifts-5', 'task': 'check_order', 'instance': 34, 'value': {'total': 80}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 52.216, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'gifts-5', 'task': 'wrap_gift', 'instance': 7, 'value': {'event_type': 'gift_wrapped'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 54.362, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'gifts-5', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 29, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_packed'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 54.362, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'gifts-5', 'task': 'ship_order', 'instance': 27, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_shipped', 'gift': 1, 'backordered': 1}}

docs.title: Upstream
docs.text:
A task started by next receives what the task before it handed on, the Upstream: the finished task's instance id, the entity's key and attributes, and its payload. A builder function gets it by declaring a parameter called upstream, and the entity by declaring entity; a function that declares neither works as before. The first task of a flow gets upstream=None.

docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:builder-upstream
# A function declaring `upstream` receives what the previous task handed on,
# and `entity` the order itself; a payload includes attributes only when it asks
@app.task()
def ship_order(task_id: int, upstream, entity):
    return {
        "event_type": "order_shipped",
        "packed_by": upstream.task_id,  # the instance of pack_order before it
        "gift": entity.attributes.get("gift"),
        "backordered": entity.attributes.get("backordered"),
    }


# A rule can also be a function of the Upstream, returning a task name or None
@app.task(next=lambda upstream: "check_order" if upstream.payload["ok"] else None)
def inspect_return(task_id: int):
    return {"ok": False}

docs.title: Example: A Flow of Tasks
docs.text:
The flow example: orders are picked, gift orders are wrapped, one parcel in ten is packed again, and every order is shipped. Wrapping and shipping are timed steps. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

Quick Start

desflow examples get downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

uvpip 
# 1. Install
uv tool install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get flow --api yaml
cd flow/yaml

# 3. Run it
desflow run flow.yaml

# 1. Install
pip install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get flow --api yaml
cd flow/yaml

# 3. Run it
desflow run flow.yaml
examples/yaml/flow.yaml:routes
tasks:
  pick:
    service: picking
    resource: pickers
    payload: {event_type: order_picked}
    # The first rule that holds wins; default catches the rest.
    next:
      when:
        - {condition: "attr.gift == 1", task: wrap}
      default: pack
  wrap:
    # A timed step: a service and no resource, so no queued event and no wait.
    service: wrapping
    payload: {event_type: gift_wrapped}
    # Applied to the entity's attributes when the task finishes.
    set: {wrapped: 1}
    next: pack
  pack:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
    # Drawn from this task's own random sequence: one parcel in ten is packed again.
    next:
      weights: {ship: 9, pack: 1}

The whole file is examples/yaml/flow.yaml.

Quick Start

# 2. Download the example
