examples/builder/flow_example.py:routes
@app.task(
    service_id="picking",
    resource_id="pickers",
    # The first rule that holds wins; default catches the rest
    next={"when": [{"condition": "attr.gift == 1", "task": "wrap"}], "default": "pack"},
)
def pick(task_id, context):
    """Picks the order's items."""
    return {"event_type": "order_picked"}


# A timed step: a service and no resource, so no queued event and no wait.
# `set` is applied to the entity's attributes when the task finishes.
@app.task(service_id="wrapping", set={"wrapped": 1}, next="pack")
def wrap(task_id, context):
    """Wraps a gift."""
    return {"event_type": "gift_wrapped"}


# Drawn from this task's own random sequence: one parcel in ten is packed again
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    next={"weights": {"ship": 9, "pack": 1}},
)
def pack(task_id, context):
    """Packs the order."""
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

The whole file is examples/builder/flow_example.py.

Quick Start

desflow examples get downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

uvpip 
# 1. Install
uv tool install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get flow --api low-level
cd flow/low-level

# 3. Run it
uv run --no-project --with desflow flow_example.py

# 1. Install
pip install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get flow --api low-level
cd flow/low-level

# 3. Run it
python flow_example.py
examples/low-level/flow_example.py:routes
ROUTES = {
    "pick": Router(
        {"when": [{"condition": "attr.gift == 1", "task": "wrap"}], "default": "pack"}
    ),
    "wrap": Router("pack"),
    # Weights draw from a generator, set in processes()
    "pack": Router({"weights": {"ship": 9, "pack": 1}}),
    "ship": Router(None),
}
SETS = {"wrap": {"wrapped": 1}}

The whole file is examples/low-level/flow_example.py.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Conditions. A condition is a Python expression, parsed with Python's ast module and checked against a list of what is allowed before it is ever evaluated; nothing goes through eval. It may use:

  • numbers, True and False, and the arithmetic +, -, *, /, // and %;
  • the comparisons <, <=, >, >=, == and !=, and strings compared with == or !=;
  • and, or, not, and the conditional form a if c else b;
  • names with their source as a prefix: payload.<field>, attr.<name>, level.<name> and registry["<path>"];
  • t, the simulation time in seconds.

A name carries its source so that adding a payload field cannot change what an attribute of the same name means, and so registry paths, which contain dots, can be written whole. Anything else is refused with a message that names it:

docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:refused
for text in ("payload.total ** 2", "x > 1", "open('orders.csv')"):
    try:
        Expression(text)
    except ValueError as error:
        print(error)

'payload.total ** 2' uses the operator Pow, which an expression cannot
'x > 1' uses the name 'x' (write payload.<field>, attr.<name>, level.<name>, registry["<path>"] or t), which an expression cannot
'open('orders.csv')' uses a Call, which an expression cannot

A blueprint is checked when it loads: every condition parses, every task a rule names exists, every level.<name> names a store or container, and every registry["..."] is a path of the model, each with its YAML line. The builder makes the same checks when run() starts. A name that is missing when a condition is evaluated, such as a payload field, raises an error naming the expression.

Weights. The weights are turned into cumulative shares once. Each choice draws one uniform number from the routing task's stream and picks the task whose share it falls in.

Starting the Next Task. When a task finishes, it applies set, builds the Upstream, asks its rules for the next task and starts it as a new SimPy process, with the same entity and the next instance id from the task's counter. An arrival that spawns the task uses the same counter, so no two runs of a task share an id. In SimPy terms, one process starting the next is the whole mechanism; SimPy and desflow describes processes.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• Flow balance. The rate into each task follows from the rates into the tasks before it and the routing shares. With weights 9 to 1 back to packing, each order is packed 1 ÷ 0.9 = 1.11 times on average, so the packers see 11% more work than there are orders.
  • Rework raises utilisation. Work the load out with the rework included, as Queues and Capacity does, or a rework loop can push a resource past full use.
  • Refused expressions. **, function calls, indexing other than registry["..."], list and dictionary literals, and bare names other than t are refused.
  • One entity, one flow. A task leads to at most one next task; splitting one order into several, or joining several into one, comes after 1.0.
  • decide is kept free. The task key decide is kept for decisions sent from outside for one entity, planned after 1.0; today it is refused like any unknown key.

docs.title: Tasks and Processes: SimulationContext
docs.text: A task is what one entity does: an order being packed, a return being logged. A process is anything else that runs over time: packers going on a break every hour, a speed that drifts, a shift plan. This page shows how to write each, what run() does with them, and what a task does step by step.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: Both are SimPy generators: functions that yield to wait. The builder and YAML write the common ones for you, and the low-level API writes them by hand. A task waits for what it needs, does its work for a sampled time, publishes an event at each step, and may lead to the next task. A process can do anything a generator can: wait, change values in the registry, publish records or start tasks.

docs.title: A Task
docs.text:
A task with a service and a resource asks for a unit of the resource, holds it for a time drawn from the service, and releases it. A task with neither takes no time and holds nothing: it publishes its payload at once, which suits an entity that only records that it happened, such as a return logged.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/tasks.yaml:task
tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing  # how long the work takes
    resource: packers  # what it holds while it works
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}  # the finished event's value
    next: print_label  # the task that follows; Task Flow has the other forms
  return_logged:
    # No service and no resource: publishes its payload at once
    payload: {event_type: return_logged}

payload is a fixed mapping. A payload that changes per entity is a Python function, called as function(task_id, context):

docs/snippets/yaml/tasks.yaml:payload-function
# also under tasks: a payload computed by a Python function
pack_with_delivery:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  # Called as choose_delivery(task_id, context) when the order gets a packer
  payload: !python shop_logic.choose_delivery
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:builder-task
@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", next="print_label")
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    # Runs when the order gets a packer, before the packing time.
    # The returned dict is the finished event's value.
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.task()  # no service and no resource: publishes at once
def return_logged(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "return_logged"}

The function is called with the task id and whatever the caller passes. It also receives entity, upstream and item by keyword when it declares a parameter of that name: the entity, what the previous task handed on, and what a store get took. A function that declares none of them works as before.

docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:low-level-task
def pack_order_process(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id, label_ids):
    """What @app.task does, by hand."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        payload = {"event_type": "order_packed"}
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        publish(payload)
    # next: print_label, a new instance for the same order
    env.process(print_label_process(env, sampler, key, next(label_ids)))

This is ordinary SimPy: packers.request() waits for a unit, env.timeout waits the service time, and leaving the with block releases the unit. env.publish_event at each step is what makes it produce records.

A task can also take from or add to a store or container (get, put), rank its requests (priority), and name the task that follows it (next); Stores and Containers, Resources and Task Flow describe each.

docs.title: A Timed Step
docs.text:
A task with a service and no resource is a timed step: work that takes time but needs nothing that can be busy, such as printing a label or waiting for a supplier. It publishes started at once, with no queued event, waits the sampled time, and publishes its finished event. Its wait is 0.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/tasks.yaml:timed-step
print_label:
  # A service and no resource: a timed step that starts at once
  service: labelling
  payload: {event_type: label_printed}
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:builder-timed-step
@app.task(service_id="labelling")  # a service and no resource: starts at once
def print_label(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "label_printed"}
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:low-level-timed-step
def print_label_process(env, sampler, key, task_id):
    """A timed step: started at once, with no queued event."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.labelling"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="print_label", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
    yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
    publish({"event_type": "label_printed"})

docs.title: Arrivals Start Tasks
docs.text:
An arrival starts one task per arrival. The loop draws a gap from the arrival's distribution, waits for that duration, starts a task for the new entity, and repeats; the task runs on its own while the loop waits for the next arrival.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/tasks.yaml:arrival
arrivals:
  # Each arrival spawns one pack_order, and one return_logged
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.2, spawn: pack_order}
  returns: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.1, spawn: return_logged}
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:builder-arrival
@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def orders(context: SimulationContext):
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        # Draws the next gap, waits for it, and returns the new entity, keyed orders-1, ...
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))  # the loop goes on at once
        task_id += 1

context.wait_for_arrival returns the new Entity, whose key is the arrival name and a counter: orders-1, orders-2. Pass it to the task with entity=. A task called without one starts an entity of its own, keyed by the task's name and a counter, such as pack_order-1. The task_id becomes the record's instance. When next or a second arrival also starts the task, take the id from context.next_instance("pack_order") instead: it is the task's one counter, which next uses too, so no two runs of the task share an id.

docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:low-level-arrival
def orders_process(env, sampler, packers):
    """What @app.arrival_loop does, by hand."""
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    label_ids = itertools.count()
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))
        key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack_order_process(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id, label_ids))
        task_id += 1

In the low-level API every loop is started once, before the run:

docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:low-level-start
env.process(orders_process(env, sampler, packers))  # start each loop once
env.process(breaks_process(env, "packers", every=50, duration=5))

docs.title: A Process
docs.text:
A process runs alongside the tasks. This one sends the packers on a 5-second break every 50 seconds:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/tasks.yaml:process
processes:
  # Called as breaks(context, resource="packers", every=50, duration=5)
  - function: !python shop_logic.breaks
    kwargs: {resource: packers, every: 50, duration: 5}
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:builder-process
def breaks(context: SimulationContext, resource: str, every: float, duration: float):
    """Takes every packer off for a break of `duration` seconds every `every` seconds."""
    path = f"{context.sim_id}.resources.{resource}.current_cap"
    registry = context.env.registry
    while True:
        yield context.env.timeout(every)
        normal = registry.get(path).value
        registry.update(path, 0)
        yield context.env.timeout(duration)
        registry.update(path, normal)


app.add_process(breaks, resource="packers", every=50, duration=5)
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:low-level-process
def breaks_process(env, resource: str, every: float, duration: float):
    """What add_process starts, by hand: a plain SimPy generator."""
    path = f"Shop.resources.{resource}.current_cap"
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(every)
        normal = env.registry.get(path).value
        env.registry.update(path, 0)
        yield env.timeout(duration)
        env.registry.update(path, normal)

Setting current_cap to 0 stops new work but not the work in progress: Resources explains what happens to busy units when a capacity drops.

docs.title: Records of a Task
docs.text:
Every event of a task carries three fields beside its value: key, the entity's key; task, the task's name; and instance, the number of this run of the task, counted from 0 for each task. The first order of the blueprint above, packed and then labelled:

[EVT] {'sim_ts': 3.672, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'queued'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 3.672, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'started'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 5.369, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_packed'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 5.369, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'print_label', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.labelling', 'status': 'started'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 7.369, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'print_label', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'event_type': 'label_printed'}}

All five events share the key orders-1, so an order can be followed through every task it passes. The finished event's value is exactly the payload. Records and Telemetry describes every field.

docs.title: What run() Does
docs.text:
run() builds everything the context describes and runs it, in this order:

Until run() is called nothing exists but the description: context.env, context.spawn and context.get_resource raise RuntimeError before it. Teardown runs in a finally block, so the last statistics are published and every sink is flushed even when the run stops with an error or Ctrl+C.

docs.title: What @app.task Does
docs.text:
@app.task turns your function into a SimPy process that does these steps, publishing a record at three of them:

  1. If it has a resource or a get, it publishes queued and asks for the resource, in the resource's queue order.
  2. Once it has the resource, it takes its get from a store or container, waiting while there is not enough.
  3. It publishes started, calls your function, and keeps what it returns as the payload. The payload is computed before the service time, so it can use the state of the simulation at that moment.
  4. It waits the service time, drawn from the live distribution.
  5. It adds its put to a store or container, waiting while there is no room, then publishes the payload as the finished event and releases the resource.
  6. It applies set to the entity's attributes, and starts the next task its next chooses, if any, as a new instance for the same entity.

A YAML task and its spawn make the same task and arrival loop that the builder code above makes. In SimPy terms each task run is one process started with env.process, and each arrival loop is another; SimPy and desflow describes processes.

docs.title: Processes and the Low-level API
docs.text: add_process(func, **kwargs) starts func(context, **kwargs) when the run starts, and a YAML processes entry does the same with a !python function. Inside it, context.env is the DynamicRealtimeEnvironment, so a process can do anything a low-level script does: context.env.timeout, context.env.registry.update, context.env.publish_event. This is how low-level code joins a builder or YAML model.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• A task holds one resource. An order that needs a picker and a packing bench at once, or a handover between them, is a process: Multi-Resource Handoffs shows how.
  • A task cannot be interrupted. Breakdowns that stop work in progress, such as a label printer that jams, need a process that catches SimPy's Interrupt: Preemptive Breakdowns.
  • A finished event is exactly the payload. It has no status or path_id unless the payload includes them.
  • Runtime helpers need a running simulation. context.spawn, context.get_resource, context.get_store, context.get_container and context.env raise RuntimeError before run(); call them inside a loop, task or process.

docs.title: Time and Pacing
docs.text: A run has two clocks, and a run can follow the wall clock, ignore it, or switch from one to the other. This page shows the clock settings, the warm-up, how long a run lasts, and which parts of the environment run on each thread.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
Simulation time is the number of seconds SimPy has advanced, starting at 0; every record carries it as sim_ts. Logical time is the date and time a record carries as timestamp: logical_start_time plus the simulation time. factor sets how simulation time relates to the wall clock, and go_live_at switches that relation once during a run. One hour of simulation time is one hour of logical time, and takes as long on the wall clock as factor says:

The settings are the same on DynamicRealtimeEnvironment, on SimulationContext and in the simulation section of a blueprint.

docs.title: Logical Start Time
docs.text:
logical_start_time is the date and time that simulation time 0 maps to; without it, the run uses the moment the environment is created. A run with a backdated start writes history:

docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:logical-start
app = SimulationContext(
    sim_id="Shop",
    factor=0.0,
    logical_start_time=datetime.now() - timedelta(days=7),  # a week of history
)

A naive datetime gives timestamps with no time zone, and a timezone-aware one gives timestamps with its offset. In a blueprint it takes now, a signed duration such as -7d, or an ISO datetime, as YAML Blueprints describes.

docs.title: Factor
docs.text:
The wall-clock duration of a stretch of the run is its simulation duration times factor:

docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:factor
live = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=1.0)  # 1 simulated second takes 1 real second
twice_as_fast = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.5)  # takes half a real second
unpaced = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)  # takes no real time at all
  • factor: 1.0 follows the wall clock: a process that waits 5 simulation seconds waits 5 real seconds. It suits a live twin feeding a dashboard.
  • factor: 0 does not wait at all: the run goes as fast as the machine allows. It suits history, tests and experiments.

docs.title: Go Live
docs.text:
factor applies until the logical clock reaches go_live_at, and from that instant the run is paced at one simulation second per real second. With a backdated logical_start_time and factor: 0, one run writes the history as fast as it can, then keeps going in real time:

docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:go-live
go_live_at = datetime.now()

env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(
    factor=0.0,  # until go_live_at
    logical_start_time=go_live_at - timedelta(days=7),
    go_live_at=go_live_at,  # from here, 1 simulated second per real second
)

A sink with when: history receives the records stamped before go_live_at, and one with when: live the rest, so the two halves can go to different places:

Parquet History, Kafka Live builds such a run.

docs.title: Warm-up
docs.text:
warmup leaves the start of a run out of what it reports. It is one time per run, in simulation seconds or a duration. No sink receives a record or telemetry stamped before it, and the built-in statistics are reset once at that moment, so they describe the rest of the run. A run without it sends everything, which is what a data generator usually wants.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/trusting_results.yaml:warmup
# Records and statistics start after the first 2 minutes; 0 keeps everything
warmup: ${WARMUP:-2 min}
docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:warmup
# No sink receives a record stamped before 10 minutes, and the statistics restart then
measured = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0, warmup="10 min")
# In the low-level API, the warm-up is set with the sinks:
# env.setup_egress(sinks, warmup=600)

The warm-up is an argument of the sinks, because it is the sinks that leave records out: env.setup_egress(sinks, warmup=600). A run with no sink has nothing to leave out, and its statistics are reset at the warm-up as well when it is set through the builder.

The warm-up drops early records; go_live_at drops nothing and only decides which sink gets each one. Trusting Results shows how to choose a warm-up length.

docs.title: Run Length
docs.text:
until is in simulation seconds. run() and a blueprint's run.until also take a duration such as "10 min", "8 hours" or "1 week"; a month counts as 30 days and a year as 365.

docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:run-length
app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
app.run(until="1 week")  # 604,800 simulation seconds; a number is seconds too

Without until, SimPy runs until no events remain, and a run with an arrival never runs out of events. Neither does any run with a sink or an ingress connector, even when its own work is done, because the environment's own processes repeat for as long as the run lasts. Give such a run an until, or stop it with Ctrl+C.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
What the environment holds. A DynamicRealtimeEnvironment is SimPy's RealtimeEnvironment with four additions: the registry at env.registry, the ingress connectors, the egress connectors with their buffers, and the statistics at env.stats.

Threads. A run uses three threads, with queues between them. Records flow from the processes to the sinks, and parameter changes flow from the sources to the registry:

  • The SimPy thread runs the model. When a process publishes a record, the record goes into a buffer for each sink, and a full buffer is handed to that sink's queue.
  • The egress thread runs the sinks' asyncio code, which drains the queues and writes to Kafka, files or databases, so network waits never stall a simulation step.
  • The ingress thread runs the sources, which put (path, value) pairs on a queue.

Processes it starts. Besides your own, the environment starts an ingress monitor, which applies queued changes every 0.1 simulation seconds; a lag monitor, which publishes system.simulation.lag_seconds every simulation second; a timed flush per sink, at a factor above 0; the statistics timer; and the warm-up reset.

Pacing and the switch. Before each event, step checks the logical clock. At the first event at or after go_live_at, it sets the factor to 1.0 and moves its two anchors, env_start and real_start, so the go-live instant counts as now; without that, the first paced event would sleep off the whole backfill. The switch happens once and always to 1.0. A go_live_at at or before logical_start_time paces the whole run, with a warning, and a run that ends before it stays unpaced. go_live_at and logical_start_time must both be naive or both timezone-aware, or the environment refuses them.

Teardown. teardown(), which run() calls in a finally block, publishes the last statistics, flushes and stops the egress connectors, then stops the ingress connectors.

SimPy and desflow. SimPy's RealtimeEnvironment takes one factor for the whole run and, with strict=True, raises an error when the model falls behind the wall clock. desflow runs without waiting at factor: 0, switches to real time at go_live_at, stamps every record with a logical time, and reports falling behind as telemetry instead of raising. SimPy and desflow compares the two.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• A run with a sink or ingress needs until, or Ctrl+C, as Run Length explains.
  • At factor: 0 no timed flush runs, so records leave a buffer when it reaches batch_size and at teardown, as Egress explains. LocalIngress follows the wall clock, so its changes can land after an unpaced run has ended; a scenario follows the simulation clock. system.simulation.lag_seconds reports 0 while the run is ahead of the wall clock.
  • warmup drops, go_live_at routes. Records before a warm-up are gone; records before go_live_at go to the sinks that take history.
  • A model slower than the wall clock falls behind at factor: 1.0 and does not catch up by skipping events; lag_seconds shows by how much.

docs.title: Ways to Write a Simulation
docs.text: desflow has three ways to write a simulation: a YAML blueprint, the builder API and the low-level API. This page says how they relate and which to choose. If you are new to desflow, start with First Simulation, which shows the same model in all three APIs side by side. Return here to look up a specific component.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
The three are layers, not alternatives. Each layer writes the one below it for you:

  • A YAML blueprint is a file. SimulationContext.from_yaml, which desflow run calls, reads it and makes the same builder calls a Python script would make, so the result is an ordinary SimulationContext.
  • The builder API, SimulationContext, collects resources, distributions, tasks and connectors through its methods and decorators. Its run() compiles them into a SimParameter, builds the environment, registers the parameters and starts the processes.
  • The low-level API is that last step written by hand: a SimParameter, a DynamicRealtimeEnvironment that registers it, and SimPy processes that use the environment's resources and publish records.

Because each layer ends in the one below, the layers mix: a blueprint can reference Python written for the builder with !python, and a builder process can use the environment directly.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: YAML Blueprint Builder API Low-level API Entry point desflow run or SimulationContext.from_yaml SimulationContext DynamicRealtimeEnvironment What you write the simulation, declared in a file; Python only for logic YAML cannot express, referenced with !python what the system looks like, with decorators for each task's steps how every event and resource operates, step by step What it does for you everything the builder does, and no Python to run publishing each task's events, requesting resources, sampling times, routing between tasks, statistics nothing: you queue, start, time out and release yourself Typical use changing rates, capacities, connectors and timed experiments between runs without editing code models whose logic is most of the program, and configuration built in code, for example from a loop what the builder does not do, such as resources created during a run

docs.title: Which to Choose
docs.text:
• YAML blueprint when the configuration is what changes between runs: a new arrival rate, another packer, a different broker, a scripted experiment. A file is easy to review and to diff, a run is one command, and a blueprint has a scenario of timed changes on the simulation clock built in. Logic that YAML cannot express goes in a Python module beside the file, as Python in a Blueprint shows.
  • Builder API when most of the program is logic and you want it in one Python file, or when you build the configuration in code.
  • Low-level API when you need what the builder does not do, or full control of every event.

YAML Blueprints, Builder API and Low-level API, the next three pages, describe each way in full.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Whichever way a simulation is written, one run goes the same way from there:

The environment holds the registry of live parameters, and the resources, stores and containers follow it. Ingress connectors change registry values from outside while the run goes on. Tasks and other processes publish events and telemetry, and egress connectors write them to their sinks on a thread of their own. The registry paths, the records, the batching and the connectors are therefore the same in all three ways, and the User Guide describes each once: Live Parameters, Ingress, Egress and Records and Telemetry.
